title: The case for and against the Cardinals bringing in CB Terrion Arnold
summary: The NFL does a great job of making news year-round. Back in the day, the season ended by Christmas, the owner’s meeting was a few weeks later in mid-January, the draft commenced in April, and training camp kicked off in July. But now? Something is going on every single month. That is well-planned out. ELATED: […]
full_text: DETROIT,MICHIGAN-NOVEMBER 27: Green Bay Packers wide receiver Dontayvion Wicks #13 catches a pass for a touchdown while guarded by Detroit Lions cornerback Terrion Arnold #6 during the second half of an NFL football game between the Green Bay Packers and the Detroit Lions in Detroit, Michigan USA, on Thursday, November 27, 2025 (Photo by Jorge Lemus/NurPhoto via Getty Images) | NurPhoto via Getty Images The NFL does a great job of making news year-round. Back in the day, the season ended by Christmas, the owner’s meeting was a few weeks later in mid-January, the draft commenced in April, and training camp kicked off in July. But now? Something is going on every single month. That is well-planned out. ELATED: GARRETT WILLIAMS AMONG LEAGUE BEST The Super Bowl is in February. Free agency begins in March, while the draft is held in April. May is the schedule release, while June is OTAs and players having over a month of time off before camp begins. Usually, athletes book a stay somewhere in the Caribbean during these 40+ off days. This downtime can create opportunities for these guys to get in trouble as well. Such is the case for cornerback Terrion Arnold. He is a very talented corner. Arnold was selected in the first round of the 2024 NFL draft by the Detroit Lions and signed a four-year, $14.3 million contract. At Alabama, he was voted First Team All-American, First Team All-SEC, First Team Freshman All-American, and First Team Freshman All-SEC in just his two years of college football. He was a favorite player of Nick Saban and his wife, Terry. Currently, he is unemployed. The Lions waived him recently on June 29. The issue? He is officially charged with four counts of kidnapping, conspiracy, and four counts of armed robbery, all felonies. Florida law enforcement documents state that Arnold came up with a plan against three men whom Arnold believed had stolen $250,000 worth of luxury goods and cash from his Airbnb in Largo, Florida. He was released from custody after posting bond, which was set at $1 million, and was ordered confined to his residence in Tallahassee. Chief Judge Christopher C. Sabella denied the state’s request to keep Arnold incarcerated until his trial and is allowing the athlete to play football as his case endures. Although the State asked for a GPS ankle bracelet, the judge ruled two weeks ago that Arnold doesn’t need to wear one. This allows him to work out for other NFL clubs. He has already been given a workout by the Houston Texans and, according to his agent, is scheduled for three more soon: the Seattle Seahawks, Indianapolis Colts, and New York Jets. Former #Lions CB Terrion Arnold has had interest from the Texans, Colts, Seahawks, and Jets, according to his agent, Nicole Lynn, who testified today. The Texans had him for a workout, and Lynn said there's a "very good likelihood" Arnold will sign with a team within the next 45… pic.twitter.com/H1z45dyHNE — Ari Meirov (@MySportsUpdate) July 10, 2026 NFL teams interested in ex-Lions cornerback Terrion Arnold revealed Should the Cardinals bring him in? Arizona already has a very good defensive backfield, especially the cornerback room. Will Johnson has shown he can cover in man at the left cornerback spot, with Denzel Burke on the other side. On the depth chart, Starling Thomas, V, and Kei’Trel Clark are listed as backups to Johnson, while Max Melton and Elijah Jones are behind Burke. Other players in this group include undrafted free agent Elijah Culp and Kalen King. DC Nick Rallis uses a lot of nickel situations for the cornerback position. That is expected to continue. Listed at the starting nickel is Garrett Williams, with Sean Murphy-Bunting and Jaden Davis as his backup. This position is where an improvement could be inserted. Such as Arnold. Arnold is just 23 years old. He has 4.5 speed with an amazing 37’ vertical jump and is very intelligent. He played in 16 games with 15 starts in his rookie season and started seven games last year before injuring his shoulder in Week 5. After surgery, he was placed on IR and returned for three games later in the season. His NFL stats: 24 games played, 22 starts, 91 total tackles, 0 tackles for loss, 18 pass defenses, 1 interception, 0 sacks, 1 fumble recovery, 90 targets, 50 completions, 55.6% completion ratio, 7 touchdowns allowed, and 7 missed tackles. As a rookie, he received votes for the “NFL Defensive Player of the Year.” In addition to Arnold’s legal issues, there is the matter of his play. Despite a very good rookie season, he has been plagued by inconsistent pass coverage, allowing over half of the passes thrown in his direction to be completed. The Lions want their corners in man coverage. He does not possess exceptional recovery speed and has a problem keeping up with speedier receivers on deep routes. Plus, he has a laundry problem. He was tied for the league lead in pass interference penalties. Seven in his rookie year alone. Going into this year’s training camp, Arnold was now the Lions’ #1 cornerback. The details about the crimes So, what exactly happened to make Arnold receive all of these charges? Arnold had rented an Airbnb in Largo, Florida, at the beginning of February with several friends. Then Arnold noticed that he had been robbed. According to the Largo Police Department report, Arnold told them what was missing was two Rolex watches, an $80,000 diamond necklace with his initials attached, four pairs of Louis Vuitton men’s shoes, several bags, a new cellphone, several Goyard bags, his Bible, and $100,000 in cash. His missing phone was pinging in Miami. His limo driver’s next gig was in Miami. A plan was concocted to set this man up using two women as the bait. Arnold contacted two longtime friends who had played D-1 college football, Lyndell Hudson and Christion Williams, who is 6’-5”, 325 pounds. The meet-up was arranged as Williams and Hudson showed up earlier and hid in a closet, armed with a pistol and a rifle. Williams pistol-whipped three men for about an hour and robbed them of their belongings. This was on Facebook Live so that Arnold could watch. That same day, Arnold told the Largo Police he wanted to close the case. Days later, he flew to the Super Bowl and was involved in related activities. He walked the runway for “Fashion Week.” In May, his daughter was born. He attended Lions mini-camp in mid-June and told reporters he “had matured” since his rookie year. The arrests These came in increments. In all, three men and two women were booked. One week later, Largo Police announced they had arrested Arnold. Arnold’s attorney came right out and stated that Arnold had nothing to do with the incident. He wasn’t in the apartment at any time, and there is no reliable evidence linking him to the allegations. It was questioned whether law enforcement would be able to prove it beyond a reasonable doubt. This is CRAZY. He is facing armed robbery and kidnapping felony charges… this is the same league that just blackballed a QB for betting on his own team in college. I’d say what Arnold is facing is much worse. — Jungle Takes (@jungletakes) July 10, 2026 He was originally charged with kidnapping and armed robbery. The Largo Police Department has already stated that the two men Arnold had assumed were the burglars were not the ones who stole the money and items. In the aftermath, Arnold has been labeled as having exceptional character and has never experienced any discipline in high school, college, or the NFL. No red flags for this young man who graduated high school with a 3.8 GPA. It has been stated that the evidence against him isn’t actually as airtight as originally offered. A lot of alternate stories are circulating about what really transpired the night of the incident. Should the Cardinals bring Arnold in? He can practice and play games the entire time this case plays out, no matter how long it takes. Then again, it is probably a lot safer to obtain an unsigned free agent still out there who is not…

title: Falcons training camp 2026: 3 roster battles to watch on defense
summary: The major intrigue on the defensive side of the ball concerns starters, not reserves, but the depth battles ahead are well worth watching at three positions in particular. While we were able to figure out five battles for depth roles on offense and probably could’ve ginned up more, things are not quite as unsettled on […]
full_text: Dec 29, 2025; Atlanta, Georgia, USA; Atlanta Falcons cornerback Cobee Bryant (37) reacts after the Falcons defeated the Los Angeles Rams at Mercedes-Benz Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Dale Zanine-Imagn Images | Dale Zanine-Imagn Images The major intrigue on the defensive side of the ball concerns starters, not reserves, but the depth battles ahead are well worth watching at three positions in particular. While we were able to figure out five battles for depth roles on offense and probably could’ve ginned up more, things are not quite as unsettled on defense, where the Falcons have a pretty clear pecking order along their defensive front and at safety. The remaining intrigue for those deep reserve roles comes at linebacker and cornerback, where there are several quality candidates fighting for only a spot or two on the final 53 man roster. We’ll get into the battles for starting jobs in more detail later this week and into training camp. Let’s dive into the reserves for now. ILB4/5 Divine Deablo is starting, while Christian Harris and Kendal Daniels will be duking it out for a starting job Harris seems likely to win, given that Daniels has not been healthy to this point. The intrigue starts after that. Rookie Harold Perkins Jr. is a versatile, intriguing talent drafted by this regime, so he’s an early favorite for a spot. JD Bertrand was valued by the last regime for his occasionally useful flashes of run defense and special teams experience. Troy Andersen looked like a potential star in the making very briefly but essentially has not played for two seasons now. Channing Tindall has shown special teams value in his own right, Malik Verdon was an intriguing conversion project moving over from safety, and Daveren Rayner fits the mold of the tall, rangy converted safety that Jeff Ulbrich seems to love. Not all of these guys will be truly competitive for a fourth or fifth role, if the Falcons even keep that many players. But there’s a mix of roles to be filled and talent on hand here that could make this one of the more interesting camp battles for final roster spots, especially if Andersen is actually healthy enough to get on the field. OLB5/6 Jalon Walker is starting, James Pearce Jr. is here but might be suspended, and new additions Azeez Ojulari and Samson Ebukam are easy picks for roster spots. Beyond that there’s only a handful of EDGE players vying for a spot or two, but they’re all worthy contenders. Cameron Thomas, who overlapped with Kevin Stefanski in Cleveland and offers quality run defense, is one of them. Bralen Trice, who was an extremely productive college pass rusher and stout run defender who missed each of the last two seasons but appears healthy now, is another. DeAngelo Malone is hoping his occasional flashes as a pass rusher and special teams value can keep him around, and Keshawn Banks excelled in the UFL enough for the Falcons to sign him. Multiple players in this group are going to have to go—at least to the practice squad—and all of them profile as solid reserves in 2026. The summer will do the separating for Atlanta. CB5/6 You have the Terrell brothers locked in, and barring a trade, Mike Hughes is here. Billy Bowman Jr. is very obviously not going anywhere and should be in line for a starting role at the nickel if he’s healthy and the Falcons don’t put Avieon Terrell there. The collection of options for one or two roles is actually kind of fascinating. You have young, promising players with upside who have to prove they belong, like 2025 undrafted free agent Malcolm Dewalt IV, 2025 UDFA Cobee Bryant, 2024 UDFA A.J. Woods, and 2023 UDFA Natrone Brooks. You have veterans looking to stick and prove they can play at a high level if called upon, like C.J. Henderson, Darren Hall, and Darnay Holmes. And finally, you have Mike Ford Jr., who is hoping to stick on the strength of his special teams contributions alone. Complicating matters, the Falcons traded for Sydney Brown, who has some experience playing the nickel from his time in Philadelphia. The Falcons could choose to keep Brown as a hybrid depth safety and insurance at corner, which would cut this competition down to a single spot that eight players would be fighting for. The number of players competing, the limited 53 man spots available, and the players here should make this one of the more intriguing down-roster battles going this August.

The Chargers relied on a four-man rush 72.6% of the time in 2025. They often used stunts and twists to game players into favorable matchups and momentum. Minter’s system asks EDGEs to maintain gap integrity, maintaining a “reacting front” – which emphasizes discipline, assignment execution, and funneling runs inside. Minter will also roll out pressure packages with three edge rushers. In 2024, Joey Bosa, Khalil Mack and Tuli Tuipulotu shared the field on 44 such dropbacks. On those snaps, they produced 10 sacks and a 22.7% sack rate. Mack was stationary at one edge spot while Tuipulotu and Bosa were moved around. Who will be the Ravens’ 5th EDGE? Adisa Isaac 30 snaps in first two seasons due to injuries Third-round investment may be the only reason he is still on the roster Kaimon Rucker 2025 UDFA, spent rookie year on practice squad 6 pressures, 1 sack last preseason Ethan Burke Undrafted rookie out of Texas Tall, long, and strong – fits versatile mold Jadaveon Clowney? title: Beatdown roundtable: favorite almost-trade in Ravens history
summary: Baltimore Beatdown is all about Almost Ravens this week! In addition to our reader-driven bracket narrowing down the biggest near-acquisitions in team history, our staff will also be providing their opinions on their favorite moves the Ravens almost pulled off. Today, we’re focusing on trades: When thinking about how it fits in team history, the […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - DECEMBER 14: Maxx Crosby #98 of the Las Vegas Raiders runs off the field after the game against the Philadelphia Eagles at Lincoln Financial Field on December 14, 2025 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Mitchell Leff/Getty Images) | Getty Images Baltimore Beatdown is all about Almost Ravens this week! In addition to our reader-driven bracket narrowing down the biggest near-acquisitions in team history, our staff will also be providing their opinions on their favorite moves the Ravens almost pulled off. Today, we’re focusing on trades: When thinking about how it fits in team history, the Ravens’ cancelled trade for Terrell Owens in 2004 is fascinating. Baltimore had just won the AFC North in 2003 on the back of – surprise, surprise – an elite defense and a punishing ground game. But rookie quarterback Kyle Boller led the league’s worst passing offense with a relatively uninspiring set of targets aside from a young Todd Heap. Adding Owens into the mix could have at least stabilized the passing game into a more effective complement to the Jamal Lewis-led rushing attack – if Boller could get him the ball. Just as interesting is the difference in philosophy from those early 2000s Ravens – imagine Eric DeCosta trading a second-round pick for a 31-year-old diva wide receiver! – Nikhil Mehta My favorite player the Ravens almost traded for is Maxx Crosby. The excitement of acquiring followed by the shocking news that the Ravens backed out of the trade days later was not a fun rollercoaster of emotions. It also brought about a cloud of negativity surrounding the team from people who thought the Ravens got “cold feet” and used medical concerns as a front to back out of the deal. However, the sheer hours of imaging Crosby in the Ravens’ defense was exciting, as was seeing him quickly embrace joining the team online. Quickly pivoting and signing Trey Hendrickson instead, while keeping their two first-round picks, was ultimately a positive for the Ravens. It’s a still a what-if to imagine what a healthy Crosby could have done in Baltimore, though. – Frank Platko My favorite player the Ravens almost traded for is Jalen Ramsey. The Ravens have tried to get Ramsey multiple times in his career. In the 2016 draft, they attempted to trade up with the Cowboys for him, but the trade fell through and the Ravens picked Ronnie Stanley (not a bad fallback option). Since then, the Ravens have been reportedly in on Ramsey multiple times, including as recently as last year when he was traded from Miami to division rival Pittsburgh. But I am thinking of 2019 when the Ravens had reportedly reached out to Jacksonville in Ramsey’s prime and nearly grabbed him. Pairing prime Ramsey with prime Marlon Humphrey might have been the NFL’s best, and most physical, cornerback duo in NFL history. Ramsey is one of my favorite corners of all time, and I’ve begged the football gods to make him a Raven since he was drafted. Alas, despite chances in 2016, 2019, 2023, and 2025, it never happened. – Zach Canter Maxx Crosby has to be my answer here. While the situation quickly devolved into ridiculous online arguments over whether or not the Ravens backed out of the trade for Crosby for nefarious reasons, the move at the time had me more excited for this team than I have been in a while. Crosby has been one of my favorite players to watch since he entered the NFL. His tenacious style of play and complete skillset on the edge would have been a perfect match in a Baltimore defense. The Ravens have not had an edge rusher of Crosby’s caliber since Terrell Suggs left the building. Signing Trey Hendrickson was a nice consolation prize after failing to acquire Crosby, but I can’t lie and say that I was not extremely disappointed when the deal fell through. In hindsight, Hendrickson plus rookie first-round guard Vega Ioane and a first-round pick next year should be a better haul for the team, but the excitement of picturing Crosby in the purple and black is hard to match. – Dustin Cox Who is the biggest Almost-Raven in franchise history? | Baltimore Beatdown
author: Dustin Cox

title: From a former Raven: why the goalposts keep moving on Lamar Jackson
summary: Baltimore Beatdown is proud to introduce this four-part series on Lamar Jackson from former Ravens running back Femi Ayanbadejo! He is a member of the 2000 Super Bowl championship team and an 11-year NFL veteran. He also holds an MBA from Johns Hopkins, with executive credentials from Harvard and Wharton, and has worked in sports […]
full_text: ARLINGTON, TX - APRIL 26: Lamar Jackson of Louisville poses after being picked #32 overall by the Baltimore Ravens during the first round of the 2018 NFL Draft at AT&T Stadium on April 26, 2018 in Arlington, Texas. (Photo by Tom Pennington/Getty Images) | Getty Images Baltimore Beatdown is proud to introduce this four-part series on Lamar Jackson from former Ravens running back Femi Ayanbadejo! He is a member of the 2000 Super Bowl championship team and an 11-year NFL veteran. He also holds an MBA from Johns Hopkins, with executive credentials from Harvard and Wharton, and has worked in sports media as an NFL analyst since 2013. Ayanbadejo is currently part of the radio team at 105.7 The Fan Baltimore. Lamar Jackson trades like a meme stock in the marketplace of media and executive opinion. His perceived value surges after an MVP season, crashes after a playoff loss, and resets with almost no institutional memory of the underlying fundamentals. The film, the production, and the total body of work change gradually. The narrative price moves overnight. Jackson is judged differently than any quarterback in recent memory. His accolades take the stairs up while his critics put him on the elevator down. Every achievement is earned slowly, scrutinized at every floor, and met at the top with a new reason it was not enough. Every criticism arrives instantly and is amplified before anyone checks whether it is true. Old narratives are zombie-like in their refusal to die. Evidence of underperformance is weighted against his entire body of work, while evidence of growth is often treated as temporary. When the facts change, the framing simply finds a new form. That narrative volatility is visible right now. In the player-voted NFL Top 100, Jackson fell 67 places—from No. 2 to No. 69—after an injury-disrupted season in which he still finished fourth in passer rating at 103.8. Trevor Lawrence ranked 62nd and Bo Nix 59th, while ESPN’s survey of more than 70 executives, coaches, and scouts placed Jackson fifth among quarterbacks. Colin Cowherd’s movement was even more revealing: he ranked Jackson seventh in May, then 11th in July, choosing the “ascending” Drake Maye over an “expensive, declining” Jackson and announcing that he was “selling his stock.” Skepticism about Jackson in major postseason moments is fair; declaring him a depreciating asset after one injury-marred season is not. He is 29. Matthew Stafford just won MVP at 37, Aaron Rodgers and Peyton Manning won at 37 or older, and Tom Brady won at 40. Meanwhile, Baltimore’s supporting cast was ranked 22nd. When Jackson produces an MVP-caliber season, critics say he is loaded with talent. When preseason rankings arrive, that same supporting cast is considered below average while Jackson’s individual value collapses. This is not consistent evaluation. It is narrative volatility. If every NFL player were available in a franchise draft today and the objective were to win now, I do not believe five players would be selected before Lamar Jackson. People underestimating Jackson is not an occasional occurrence. It is his norm. The hyperbole surrounding him since before the draft has helped create a man largely impervious to nonsensical commentary. He rarely responds to it. I will. View this post on Instagram I write from the intersection of athlete, analyst, admiration, and accountability. Not all criticism of Jackson is invalid. His decision-making in several playoff losses, his postseason ball security, and a 3-5 playoff record are fair subjects for scrutiny. This series addresses them directly. What is not fair is the pattern of unverified character attacks, manufactured destination narratives, and lazy analysis that presents subjective opinion with the authority of sourced fact. Over the past year, the pile-on has been particularly pointed. Emmanuel Acho called Jackson the “common denominator” in Baltimore’s postseason failures and expressed no confidence that he would ever win a Super Bowl. Eric Mangini questioned his maturity and loyalty. Greg Cote invoked Dan Marino as a cautionary comparison. Mike Preston published a commentary containing character allegations and destination speculation without disclosing a verifiable source. These claims do not all belong in the same category. Some are legitimate opinions. Some contain valid questions. Others are unsupported assertions. Responsible analysis requires us to distinguish among them. Before He Ever Took a Snap The underestimation of Lamar Jackson did not begin in the NFL. It began before he was drafted, in one of the most polarizing quarterback evaluations of the modern era. During the 2018 pre-draft cycle, scouts and media figures questioned whether Jackson’s college game at Louisville could translate to the NFL. Former Indianapolis Colts general manager Bill Polian publicly argued that Jackson lacked the size and accuracy to remain at quarterback and should move to wide receiver. Multiple teams asked Jackson to go through receiver drills at the Scouting Combine. He refused, participating only as a quarterback. Critics emphasized his sub-60 percent college completion rate, called him raw, and questioned whether his rushing style could survive professional football. Ozzie Newsome evaluated the same player differently. In his final draft as Ravens general manager, Newsome traded back into the first round and selected Jackson 32nd overall. He did not know precisely what Jackson would become. He recognized that the prevailing evaluation placed too much weight on convention and too little on exceptional ability: rare acceleration, arm strength, a quick release, spatial awareness, and the capacity to stress every defender on the field. No one could know that Jackson would become a multiple-time MVP and redefine the geometry of the position. Newsome simply gave an unconventional quarterback the opportunity to be evaluated as a quarterback. That decision became one of the defining selections in franchise history. The Moving Goalposts The doubt did not stop when Jackson entered the league. It evolved whenever the evidence defeated its previous form. First, he could not play quarterback in the NFL. Then he could win only with his legs and was not a “real passer.” Next, he could succeed only in a specialized offense with simplified reads. Then he won MVP awards in two distinct offensive structures: Greg Roman’s zone-read-heavy, historically productive rushing system in 2019 and Todd Monken’s more expansive passing structure in 2023. From Marty Mornhinweg to Roman to Monken, the coordinator changed. The system changed. The personnel changed. Jackson kept winning and developing. He has answered nearly every threshold placed in front of him. One remains unresolved: whether he can consistently protect the football and deliver his best football through a complete championship run. At least now we are discussing something real. What This Series Is Belief is subjective. Truth is not. A belief can be sincere and still be wrong. Quantitative claims require data. Qualitative claims require verification. Those who claim to know what a player thinks, feels, or intends while that player stays silent are not analyzing. They are guessing. This series does not argue that Lamar Jackson is beyond criticism. It argues that criticism should be specific, proportionate, and supported by evidence. Part Two takes the conversation to the field and examines what the film and data actually establish, including the postseason criticism Jackson and the Ravens have earned. Part Three examines the off-field narratives: representation, contract leverage, character allegations, destination rumors, and the media ecosystem that converts speculation into received wisdom. Part Four considers what Jackson has already changed, what remains unfinished, and how his remaining career could reshape his legacy. The standard will remain the same throughout: verified fact, supported inference, clearly identified…

title: Bring on your best Buffalo Bills tailgating ideas
summary: Hey everyone! It’s your favorite (bold assumption but I’m making it) recipe writer here, looking to get you into the game. The food game. Okay, just the food writing game. I think you get the idea. I want you to tell me recipes you’d like to see my take on and I’ll compile your ideas, […]
full_text: Hey everyone! It’s your favorite (bold assumption but I’m making it) recipe writer here, looking to get you into the game. The food game. Okay, just the food writing game. I think you get the idea. I want you to tell me recipes you’d like to see my take on and I’ll compile your ideas, choose ones I like, and give you a shoutout if I write yours up. Oh yeah, you can count on me doing something zany and weird with the idea too. It’s kind of my brand. What are you talking about weirdo? Weirdo? Do you know who you’re talking to with that heading posed as a hypothetical question from the reader? I’m the creator of the Zubazgel, and don’t you forget it! This was easily my favorite creation from last season’s recipes. For those of you new to the site, each year I do recipes based on the Bills and their opponent for every week of the regular and postseason. Sometimes they get weird, and often the food is pretty good if you want to try it out. Here’s the Zubazgel recipe if you’re curious. Once in awhile there’s even a really good idea. Like my Sloppy Joe variant that’s way cleaner to eat than usual thanks to the addition of onion rings. It’s called the “Tidy Joey” I’m not just simply stretching my word count with these, but attempting to get your creative ideas swirling too. Swirling like this insanely glittery drink I concocted . In all seriousness, these ideas are here to show the breadth of what you’re free to suggest. Simple cocktails can become surprisingly fun in the right hands. Engineering applied to sandwiches, or finding out just how “mixing averse” dough can be toward itself are just some of the oddities we’ve had a blast with over the years. For longtime readers, you know the original goal was to always have a strong tie-in with the opposing team and that’s certainly still fair game. That said, I’ve been doing these since Week 1 of the 2018 season. By my count that’s 148 games, and roughly that many recipes (I doubled up once during COVID and have made a couple special editions over the years). What I’m getting at is that I’ve done all sorts of things already and gotten into some deep dives for research purposes. If I can find a tie-in with the opponent, I will. If not, let’s still have some fun with it. Let me know in the comments what recipe you might want to see me butcher!
author: Skarekrow

title: Did Brandon Beane and the Buffalo Bills get ahead of the linebacker market?
summary: When reports that the Buffalo Bills signed linebacker Terrel Bernard to a four-year, $50 million extension in March 2025, the reaction from portions of Bills Mafia was mixed. As real contract numbers slowly surfaced, the deal was a four-year, $42 million contract with some escalators and “not like to be earned” bonuses. Fast forward to […]
full_text: HOUSTON, TX - NOVEMBER 20: Terrel Bernard #8 of the Buffalo Bills exits the field at halftime during an NFL football game against the Houston Texans at NRG Stadium on November 20, 2025 in Houston, Texas. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images When reports that the Buffalo Bills signed linebacker Terrel Bernard to a four-year, $50 million extension in March 2025, the reaction from portions of Bills Mafia was mixed. As real contract numbers slowly surfaced, the deal was a four-year, $42 million contract with some escalators and “not like to be earned” bonuses. Fast forward to the end of the 2025 season, and any of the positivity derived had seemingly vanished altogether. Some questioned whether general manager Brandon Beane had moved too quickly. Bernard was coming off consecutive 100 tackle seasons and had established himself as the leader of Buffalo’s defense, but injuries limited his effectiveness in 2025. Was paying him $10.5 million per season an overreaction? On Tuesday, the Miami Dolphins agreed to a three-year, $51.3 million extension with Jordyn Brooks, including $35 million guaranteed . The contract keeps Brooks in Miami through the 2029 season and makes him one of the NFL’s highest-paid linebackers at $17.1 million per year. The comparison between the two contracts is striking. While Brooks received just $9.3 million more in total contract value, he’s earning $6.6 million more per season on average than Bernard. Had Bernard reached this offseason healthy and produced another 100-plus tackle campaign, it’s fair to wonder whether his asking price would have climbed much closer to Brooks’ range. To be fair, Brooks has earned every bit of his new contract. The former first round pick is coming off a spectacular 2025 season in which he led the NFL with 183 tackles, had 3.5 sacks, 13 tackles for loss, forced a fumble, and earned First-Team All-Pro honors for the first time in his career. Bernard’s résumé isn’t quite as decorated. Not even close. What he represents however, is something the Bills value philosophically; develop, lead, extend. That’s been their trademark in the Beane era. Since taking over as Buffalo’s starting middle linebacker, Bernard has become the quarterback of the Bills defense. He’s been voted one of the team’s captains in each of the past two seasons alongside Josh Allen. He produced back-to-back 100 tackle seasons while healthy in 2023 and 2024. But injuries slowed him in 2025, dropping his production almost by half. The Bills weren’t paying solely for statistics. They were investing in one of the leaders of their locker room, a player they believe is entering his prime, and one they wanted to keep in Buffalo before the market had another chance to reset. It’s a strategy Beane has used repeatedly. Rather than waiting for players to reach free agency or produce career years, Buffalo has often signed foundational pieces early. Christian Benford, Khalil Shakir, Greg Rousseau, and Bernard all fit that philosophy. But, is it the right move? You never know until it plays out. Looking at Brooks’ extension, it’s becoming easier to understand the timing. If Bernard returns to his 2023 and 2024 form this season, a $10.5 million annual salary could quickly look like one of the better values among starting linebackers. Had Buffalo waited until 2026, they might have been negotiating in a market where Brooks’ $17.1 million annual average had become an obvious benchmark. If Bernard returns to being the every-down captain who routinely topped 100 tackles and anchored the defense, Beane’s decision to extend him early could prove to be outstanding value. If injuries continue to limit his availability or production, the questions surrounding the contract will only grow louder. The truth is, we still don’t know whether Beane got a bargain or paid a premium for Bernard. That answer won’t come from comparing contracts just yet. It’ll come from Bernard’s performance over the next 17 games. For Bills fans, if he has a great season, contract numbers rarely matter. For now, the Bills’ decision remains incomplete. The contract has been signed for a while now, but the final grade won’t be written until Bernard shows whether he can stay healthy and perform like one of the league’s top linebackers.
author: Sara Larson

title: Underrated Buffalo Bills who I expect to make noise at 2026 training camp
summary: At St. John Fisher University, there will be underrated Buffalo Bills players who string together multiple strong training camp practices en route to a buzz-generating summer. This phenomenon happens every year at training camps across the NFL. These are the underrated, bottom-half-of-the-roster Bills I expect to have quality camps which will be parlayed into larger […]
full_text: CLEVELAND, OH - DECEMBER 21: Buffalo Bills linebacker Joe Andreessen (44) leaves the field following the National Football League game between the Buffalo Bills and Cleveland Browns on December 21, 2025, at Huntington Bank Field in Cleveland, OH. (Photo by Frank Jansky/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images At St. John Fisher University, there will be underrated Buffalo Bills players who string together multiple strong training camp practices en route to a buzz-generating summer. This phenomenon happens every year at training camps across the NFL. These are the underrated, bottom-half-of-the-roster Bills I expect to have quality camps which will be parlayed into larger roles during the 2026 season. EDGE Javon Solomon It’s now or never for Solomon who enters Year 3 after being selected by the Bills in the fifth round of the 2024 draft. Remember his collegiate campaign culminated with a 16-sack season Troy in 2023. Solomon was always a strange fit as a defensive end in Sean McDermott’s defense, a scheme that prioritized size and length at the position, two clearly lacking aspects of Solomon’s physical profile — he’s listed at 6’1’ and 246 pounds. But that frame is much closer to what Jim Leonhard presumably wants for the rush linebacker role in his scheme. He coached the 6’2”, 240-pound Nick Herbig at Wisconsin and was on the sidelines in Denver during the emergence of the 6’3, 248-pound Nik Bonitto. Solomon has appeared on 12.1% and 19.8% of Buffalo’s defensive snaps in his first two seasons, and by now, he’s likely amassed NFL-caliber strength so he’s not as easily overwhelmed in the run game. Then again, I believe Solomon’s splash plays in camp will come as one of the few designated pass rushers (on the outside) on Buffalo’s roster. Despite being on the small / short side for the position, Solomon’s arm length is in the 65th percentile for the EDGE position. Do I expect Solomon to earn a starting rush linebacker gig after St. John Fisher University this summer? No. But this is when he makes enough of an impact there to earn spot duty as a pass-rush specialist in the regular season. RB Ian Wheeler Going out on a limb here, as I don’t know a ridiculous amount about Wheeler, and he was just added to the Bills roster in mid June. I don’t adore the RB3 options currently on the Bills roster — and wrote a column about why I believe Ty Johnson should be Buffalo’s RB2 ahead of Ray Davis in 2026. Frank Gore Jr. did catch a pass in the wild-card win over the Jaguars. I’m not quite ready to predict a giant leap forward for him as a runner. I’m not completely done with Ray Davis, either. But close. I think his best path to contributing on the Bills is as a returner. Without a veteran signing or even a late-round draft selection at running back, Wheeler has as good of an opportunity to earn an eventual spot on a gameday roster as any mid-June acquisition. Here’s the type of athlete the Bills got in Wheeler, who won the UFL United Bowl MVP just a few months ago: Dude can scoot and has NFL-caliber juice once he touches the football. I expect Wheeler to be a training camp all-star and accumulate plenty of yardage — often on chunk plays — during the third and fourth quarter of preseason games this August. LB Joe Andreessen Andreessen hasn’t been discussed enough in the (potential) open gig(s) at inside linebacker in Leonhard’s scheme. We all expect Terrel Bernard to land one of the those jobs. I like Dorian Williams to start Week 1 next to him. But Andreessen has paid his dues on special teams, has been a preseason star for two seasons now, and is one of the most physically gifted linebackers on the roster at 6’1” and a hefty 240 pounds. He’s the exact type of developmental project the Bills have cultivated many times during the Brandon Beane era, and I expect Buffalo’s defensive staff to give him opportunities to prove himself with the backups at some stages during training camp. And I expect Andreessen to be up to the task. With more condensed responsibilities between the tackles, Andreessen can more narrowly focus on attacking the football on run plays and disrupting the backfield when the opposing quarterback drops back to pass. We all remember Andreessen erupting onto the scene in August 2024 en route to making the 53-man roster as a UDFA from Lancaster and University at Buffalo. I envision Andreessen’s name being mentioned as a stock-up player in many training camp recaps this summer. He’s ready. TE Jackson Hawes Anyone else feel a mini-breakout looming for Hawes in Year 2? The run-down monster quietly averaged 1.82 yards per route run on 102 routes as a rookie. And, sure, the low sample size much be considered with that elite-level figure, but it does hint at receiving promise for the devastating blocker. Of course, Hawes has mainstays Dalton Kincaid and Dawson Knox ahead of him on the tight end depth chart, yet if the Bills decide to limit Kincaid’s workload, Hawes will be taking plenty of reps with the No. 1 offense. Heck, he played on 43% of the snaps in his rookie season. Could that number eclipse 50% in 2026? Absolutely… even if Kincaid stays reasonably healthy. Hawes should demonstrate enough athleticism and sure-handedness in camp to garner more looks in the pass game — mostly underneath — when the games actually count. Plus, his presence on the field won’t telegraph Buffalo’s play intentions as much as Kincaid. While league rules don’t allow much physicality in training camp anymore, Hawes’ true strength won’t be on full display in Pittsford. The noise he makes will be as a receiver, and that’s where the most potential growth resides for this soon-to-be 26-year-old tight end. S/NCB/LB Wande Owens In May, I wrote on my fascination with Owens because he was a 2025 undrafted free agent who was injured for his rookie season but the team decided to retain him for his second NFL season. Probably because he’s a spectacular athlete. These were Owens’ numbers at his pro day before the 2025 NFL Draft: 40-Yard Dash: 4.58 seconds (41st percentile) 10-Yard Split: 1.53 seconds (69th) Vertical: 43 inches (98th) Broad Jump: 135 inches(97th) Three-Done : 6.99 seconds (53rd) Short-Shuttle: 4.05 seconds (87th) At Yale and New Hampshire Owens aligned free safety, strong safety, linebacker, and nickel corner at 5’11” and 205 pounds. He’s another player who may very well benefit from the defensive overhaul which is almost guaranteed to include a new role under Leonhard’s watchful eye. It’ll likely be during the second and third team periods, but I expect Owens to be a magnet to the football in those sessions because of his athleticism, instincts, and tackling reliability.
author: Chris Trapasso

title: Buffalo Bills 2026 scouting report: wide receiver Trent Sherfield
summary: The Buffalo Bills have fourteen wide receivers in camp, which is more players than they have at any single position right now. Buffalo will likely keep just six of those receivers, and that’s assuming that they don’t sign or trade for someone else before final roster cuts happen at the end of August. For the […]
full_text: MIAMI GARDENS, FLORIDA - JANUARY 07: Trent Sherfield #16 of the Buffalo Bills catches a touchdown pass during the second quarter against the Miami Dolphins at Hard Rock Stadium on January 07, 2024 in Miami Gardens, Florida. (Photo by Rich Storry/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills have fourteen wide receivers in camp, which is more players than they have at any single position right now. Buffalo will likely keep just six of those receivers, and that’s assuming that they don’t sign or trade for someone else before final roster cuts happen at the end of August. For the top-end of the depth chart, each receiver’s clear role is to be a weapon in the passing game. For those players looking to make the team at the back end of the roster, they’ll need to do more than that to show that they belong. Supporting in the run game as a blocker is one thing, but for those last players on the roster, showing up and showing out on special teams is a must for inclusion on the 53-man roster. In today’s edition of “91 players in 91 days,” we discuss a veteran wideout looking to return to the Bills’ roster after a one-year stint with the club in 2023. _____________________________________________________________________________ Name: Trent Sherfield Number: 81 Position: WR Height/Weight: 6’1” 205 lbs. Age: 30 (31 on 2/26/2027) Experience/Draft: 9; signed with the Arizona Cardinals following the 2018 NFL Draft College: Vanderbilt Acquired: Signed with Buffalo on 3/26/2026 Financial situation (per Spotrac): Sherfield signed a one-year contract at the veteran’s minimum, which is $1.3 million for the season. Thanks to the veteran’s salary benefit, Sherfield’s cap hit if he makes the team is a bit lower at $1.075 million. If he’s released prior to wee one, Buffalo will carry no dead cap charge; however, as a vested veteran, Sherfield’s $1.3 million base salary becomes fully guaranteed if he’s on the roster for Buffalo’s first game. 2025 Recap: Last spring, Sherfield signed a two-year deal with the Denver Broncos for a total of $8 million. $1.5 million of that contract was guaranteed. He played in 10 games for Denver, starting three. He caught just three passes for 21 yards on four targets. Heading into Denver’s Week Eleven matchup with the Kansas City Chiefs, they signed Lil’Jordan Humphrey to the active roster and released Sherfield. He signed with the Cardinals’ practice squad on November 19, and he was elevated for two games. He saw one target in those contests. With both teams, he primarily appeared on special teams. After the Cardinals’ season ended without a playoff berth, Sherfield was not offered a reserve/futures contract—or chose not to accept an offered deal—and he became a free agent. He signed with the New England Patriots’ practice squad on January 13; with the Pats awaiting the winner of a Bills-Broncos Divisional Round game, Sherfield could provide intel on both clubs. He was not elevated for the Patriots’ AFC Championship Game victory, and he was released from the practice squad on January 24. He re-signed with New England’s practice squad on January 28, but he was not elevated for their loss in the Super Bowl to the Seattle Seahawks. Positional outlook: Sherfield is one of 14 wideouts on the current roster. Khalil Shakir, DJ Moore, Keon Coleman, Joshua Palmer, Skyler Bell, Mac Dalena, Ja’Mori Maclin, Mecole Harman Jr., Stephen Gosnell, Jalen Virgil, Quentin Skinner, Tyrell Shavers, and Max Tomczak are the others. 2026 Offseason: Sherfield is healthy and participating in offseason work as both a receiver and a special teams gunner. 2026 Season outlook: Signing a receiver like Trent Sherfield isn’t a move meant to solidify the top end of the receiver room. After all, he’s been in the NFL for eight years and his career receiving line (89 catches, 1,034 yards, 6 touchdowns) reads like a single season for a normal WR1 than it does a full career. That’s not necessarily a knock on Sherfield, either, as each player brings unique talents to a room, and each part of the positional group has a role to fill. Sherfield’s role isn’t to replicate what someone like Stefon Diggs meant to Buffalo’s receiver room; instead, it’s meant to replicate what Tyrell Shavers meant to that same group. The irony, perhaps, is that 2025 Tyrell Shavers was really playing the role of 2023 Trent Sherfield. That is, he was a wide receiver whose main function came on special teams, and who could see some run and some targets on offense as an auxilliary piece in certain formations. Shavers, to be fair, showed a little more as a receiver and a lot more as a blocker than Sherfield. If Sherfield is going to stick with Buffalo this season, it’s going to be as the sixth wideout in a special teams-heavy role. He’ll be facing off against veterans like Mecole Hardman Jr. and Jalen Virgil as his primary competition for that spot. None of those players offers much in the form of receiving ability, and one could actually make the argument that Sherfield is the best actual pass-catcher of that group at this point in their respective careers. Depending on the coaching staff’s preference, I imagine that one of those three players will be the last man on the roster. Sherfield has a shot at the 53-man roster this season, but he’ll have to attack his role and show some versatility in order to lock in down.
author: Sean Murphy

title: Three potential Panthers starters placed on injury lists
summary: On Wednesday, the Carolina Panthers made a series of roster moves in preparation for training camp, which officially started today. The moves: The trio join Jaycee Horn and Taylor Moton, who were reportedly destined for the NFI list on Tuesday. Horn and Brown aren’t expected to miss much time. Brown’s hamstring injury is considered pretty […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - NOVEMBER 09: Ikem Ekwonu #79 of the Carolina Panthers enters the field before an NFL game against the New Orleans Saints at Bank of America Stadium on November 09, 2025 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by David Jensen/Getty Images) | Getty Images On Wednesday, the Carolina Panthers made a series of roster moves in preparation for training camp, which officially started today. The moves: Ikem Ekwonu was placed on the PUP list as he recovers from a torn patella tendon suffered in the playoffs Tershawn Wharton was placed on the PUP list as he recovers from neck surgery Bobby Brown III was placed on the non-football injury list with a hamstring injury The trio join Jaycee Horn and Taylor Moton, who were reportedly destined for the NFI list on Tuesday. Horn and Brown aren’t expected to miss much time. Brown’s hamstring injury is considered pretty mild, and Horn simply got a cut on his foot that required stitches. The other three are more up in the air. Moton’s reportedly been undergoing treatment for his blood clots for about a month, and it seems as though that’s going to continue through the start of the season. Ekwonu’s apparently been doing very well in his rehab, but a torn patella tendon is a serious injury, and it’ll be a major accomplishment if he’s ready at any point this season. Wharton’s neck injury is a total mystery for us on the outside, but it seems like he’s expected to be ready at some point this season. Between Moton and Ekwonu’s health issues, it’s a good thing the Panthers invested a first round pick in Monroe Freeling in the 2026 NFL Draft. He and Rasheed Walker look penciled in to be the Panthers starters at tackle for the foreseeable future. As for the roster designations, there’s functionally little difference between the PUP and NFI lists. In either case, players must start camp on one of the two lists. They can’t be placed on either after they’ve played or practiced. They count against the 90 player limit during the offseason and can be activated at any time. If they stay on either list through roster cutdowns, they must miss at least the first four games of the regular season, though they don’t count against the 53 man roster limit at that point. The only difference between the two lists is the nature of what lands a player on one or the other. The PUP is for players recovering from injureis suffered during NFL play. The NFI list is for injuries sustained outside of NFL activities (like Horn) or for other illnesses (like Moton). It’s not the worst start to camp in terms of injury luck. Fingers crossed and knock on wood that it doesn’t get worse from here.

title: Panthers Reacts Survey: What do we expect from Brady Christensen this year?
summary: This was a question we wanted to ask before we learned of Taylor Moton’s recent medical situation. Christensen has long been both a versatile offensive lineman and a fan favorite. With Moton set to miss an unspecified amount of time this season, Christensen’s availability and progress are of even greater interest t0 the Panthers. Christensen […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NC - OCTOBER 26: Carolina Panthers offensive lineman Brady Christensen (70) during an NFL football game between the Buffalo Bills and the Carolina Panthers on October 26, 2025 at Bank of America Stadium in Charlotte, N.C. (Photo by John Byrum/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images This was a question we wanted to ask before we learned of Taylor Moton’s recent medical situation. Christensen has long been both a versatile offensive lineman and a fan favorite. With Moton set to miss an unspecified amount of time this season, Christensen’s availability and progress are of even greater interest t0 the Panthers. Christensen has played in 59 games in his five seasons with the Panthers, including 34 starts. Six of those starts have been at tackle (all in 2021) and 28 have been across both guard positions in the years since. It is unclear if Moton’s pending absence affected the Panthers decision to bring Christensen back beyond their interest in him as somebody who can back up all five positions along the offensive line. There is also Christensen’s own recovery from injury to consider. He tore his Achilles tendon in Week 8 of the 2025 season. The typical timeline for returning from such an injury would have him practicing within as little as eight months and playing in games again as late as a year later. Many athletes also never return to their full pre-injury form after an Achilles tear. Christensen was cleared for contact this summer before the Panthers signed him, so presumably he is well on the road to recovery. When and where that road will end, however, is a question that remains to be answered. Now we turn the larger question of his future over to you, Panthers fans. What do you expect from Brady Christensen this year? Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Panthers fans and fans across the country. Sign up here to participate in the weekly emailed surveys.

title: 2026 Season Opener Countdown: 53 Days Remaining
summary: Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to […]
full_text: ATLANTA - DECEMBER 18: Punter Todd Sauerbrun #10 of the Carolina Panthers looks on against the Atlanta Falcons on December 18, 2004 at the Georgia Dome in Atlanta, Georgia. The Falcons defeated the Panthers 34-31 in overtime.(Photo by Streeter Lecka/Getty Images) | Getty Images Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to change that up a bit by counting down our own list of the Top 100 Panthers of all time. This does not correspond to jersey number, does not need to be somebody who wore a jersey, and will in no way be controversial. #53. Todd Sauerbrun One of the most fun things in football is when a player that should not be the center of attention makes themselves the center of attention. The Carolina Panthers had that with punter Todd Sauerbrun, for better or for worse. He was the best punter in franchise history, but he might be more remembered for his antics and personality than his actual play on the field. Sauerbrun came into the NFL as a second ( 2nd! ) round pick of the Chicago Bears. He spent five years there before playing one year in Kansas City. He signed with the Panthers in 2001, and boy did he time in perfectly. The Panthers had an absolutely abysmal offense in Sauerbrun’s first two seasons, which gave the burly punter plenty of opportunities to bomb punts. He was top three in the league in total punts (sick brag) and led the league in total punt yards in both seasons. He was a first team all pro in both of those seasons, then followed that up with a second team all pro in the following season. The 2004 season saw his production dip just a smidge while the off field issues start to become too much to deal with. He departed after that season and went on to be other people’s problem. In 2004, Panthers kicker John Kasay got hurt, which set off a whole host of problems with Sauerbrun. First, Sauerbrun pressured the team to not sign their preferred replacement Bill Gramatica because he disliked the entire Gramatica family. Then, he offered to pull double duty, but only on the condition that the Panthers forgive some of the money they had fined him for being overweight. That obviously didn’t go over well. Then, to make matters worse, he was arrested for driving while intoxicated late in the season. He was also linked to the Panthers steroid scandal a couple months later. You can’t have that many distractions from your punter, no matter how he good he is. While Sauerbrun had more than his fair share of troubles and controversies, he was still the best punter the Panthers have ever had. Being the best ever at your position earns you a spot in the Panthers’ top 100, even if you’re kind of a jerk.

title: Bears’ Loveland Lands on NFLPA’s “Rising Stars List”
summary: An offseason of both acknowledgment and rising expectations continues for Bears’ TE Colston Loveland. After being featured among the top 10 players at his position earlier this summer, the 2nd year man can now be found alongside a group of both rookies and veterans poised to make an impact on the retail market. This comes […]
full_text: Jun 9, 2026; Lake Forest, IL, USA; Chicago Bears tight end Colston Loveland speaks during Minicamp at Halas Hall. Mandatory Credit: Kamil Krzaczynski-Imagn Images | Kamil Krzaczynski-Imagn Images An offseason of both acknowledgment and rising expectations continues for Bears’ TE Colston Loveland. After being featured among the top 10 players at his position earlier this summer, the 2nd year man can now be found alongside a group of both rookies and veterans poised to make an impact on the retail market. This comes via the NFLPA’s annual “Rising Stars List”, which “forecasts [the] next wave of players expected to drive fan demand and merchandise sales.” As mentioned, the list highlights both rookies and veteran players, with Loveland appearing alongside notable veterans such as Las Vegas Raiders TE Brock Bowers, Buffalo Bills RB James Cook, and New England Patriots DB Christian Gonzalez. Unsurprisingly, the rookie side of the list features a number of highly-drafted players in some big markets, such as Las Vegas Raiders QB Fernando Mendoza, Dallas Cowboys S Caleb Downs, and New York Giants LB Arvell Reese. Loveland’s marketability can be debated, but there’s certainly a strong case to be made in his favor. His strong performance on the field, the home market of Chicago, and the charisma he’s displayed both on and off the field likely serve as the foundation of his place on this list. Heck, he’s even going to be featured in the upcoming Bears-centric Hallmark movie ! This list serves as the latest endorsement of Loveland, and those of us with a rooting interest in the Chicago Bears can only hope that his play in the upcoming season is reflective of all of these offseason expectations. You can check out the full NFLPA Rising Stars List here .

title: Chicago Bears’ Young Talent Named Among the NFL’s Best
summary: The Chicago Bears, coming off of a successful 2025 campaign, appear poised for a multi-year run of contention due to the amount of young talent on the team. It all starts up front with QB Caleb Williams (24 years old), but he’s far from the only young building block that GM Ryan Poles has assembled. […]
full_text: The Chicago Bears , coming off of a successful 2025 campaign, appear poised for a multi-year run of contention due to the amount of young talent on the team. It all starts up front with QB Caleb Williams (24 years old), but he’s far from the only young building block that GM Ryan Poles has assembled. The list of budding stars under 25 is lengthy: Colston Loveland (22), Rome Odunze (24), Luther Burden III (22), Dillon Thieneman (21), Darnell Wright (24), and Austin Booker (23), to name a few. That’s a heck of a young core that will only continue to get better. ESPN took notice in their recent “Ranking NFL teams by under-25 talent” list. The Bears came in at number three, trailing only last year’s Super Bowl runner-up New England Patriots and the Houston Texans. Here was their methodology for the list: Number of starts made by players under 25 years old Number of snaps played by players under 25 years old Quality of play by players under 25 years old, age-adjusted to capture the fact that a 21-year-old player of X ability will likely improve more than a 23-year-old player of X ability — and with extra consideration given to Pro Bowl and All-Pro selections Value and length of player contracts Relative importance of positions, with quarterbacks being more important and running backs, off-ball linebackers and specialists being less important than other positions Draft value added in the 2026 draft, particularly in the first three rounds Expected key starters and reserves under 25 years old for teams in 2026 Significant injuries or suspensions that will affect the 2026 availability of players under 25 years old Here’s what they had to say about the Bears: Once again, the most important young talent a team can have is at quarterback. And the Bears have a budding star in Williams, who threw for 3,942 yards and 27 touchdowns in 2025. He will be 25 on Nov. 18. His top targets are all under 25, as well. Odunze is 24, while Luther Burden III and Loveland are still just 22. Even the backups to those guys are young; the Bears used third-round picks on tight end Sam Roush and wide receiver Zavion Thomas , also both 22. Elsewhere on the roster, you will find left tackle Ozzy Trapilo , who is 24 but was discounted a bit because of a torn patellar tendon that will cost him part of this season. Defensive tackle Gervon Dexter Sr. is 24, and last year’s second-round pick, edge rusher Shemar Turner , is 23. This year’s draft picks add more impact youth, headlined by safety Dillon Thieneman (age 22) and center Logan Jones (24). One notable fact is that they didn’t consider Darnell Wright for the Bears when making the list, as he will turn 25 in just a couple of weeks. He was listed as a “graduated player.” What do you think? Patriots, Texans, then the Bears? Let us know in the comments section below!
author: Ryan Droste

title: Training Camp Battle: EDGE2: Austin Booker vs Dayo Odeyingbo
summary: We have just a couple more training camp battles to look at before the Bears report to training camp next week. Let’s pivot back to the defense and focus on the line, which has a lot of questions and potentially not a lot of answers. Even though there may not be answers, there may not […]
full_text: CHICAGO, IL - JANUARY 18: Austin Booker #94 of the Chicago Bears during an NFL divisional playoff football game on January 18, 2026 at Soldier Field in Chicago, Illinois. (Photo by Melissa Tamez/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images We have just a couple more training camp battles to look at before the Bears report to training camp next week. Let’s pivot back to the defense and focus on the line, which has a lot of questions and potentially not a lot of answers. Even though there may not be answers, there may not be many battles either. Grady Jarrett and Gervon Dexter seem set as the team’s top two DTs. Neville Gallimore seems like the team’s DT3. Sure, Bears fans would like to see Jordan van den Berg emerge as the team’s DT4 over Kentavius Street, but that’s not really worth column inches. At Edge, we know Montez Sweat holds down the top spot. Daniel Hardy will be the team’s EDGE5, who will largely play special teams. Shemar Turner is one big question mark. At this point, it’s tough to know who he is even in competition with, but who is starting opposite Sweat? The answer is probably Austin Booker, but you can’t really eliminate Dayo Odeyingbo, especially if he’s motivated (when does the joke get old? Are we there yet?) Last year, Booker and Odeyingbo were like two ships passing in the night. Booker was injured to start the year and didn’t work his way back to the active roster until November 2nd. November 2nd was the game when Odeyingbo tore his Achilles and went down for the year. Booker tallied 35 tackles and 4.5 sacks in 10 games. He also added 18 pressures. In 8 games, Odeyingbo had just 21 tackles and 1 sack with just 6 total pressures. Booker’s play in 2025 clearly was better than Odeyingbo’s. But sometimes in the NFL, money talks. Why is Deshaun Watson in the driver’s seat to start at quarterback in Cleveland? It’s certainly not his play on the field. It’s money. The Bears guaranteed Odeyingbo $31 million when they signed him to a 3-year, $48 million contract. Yes, they can and almost certainly will get out of his contract after this season, but Odeyingbo has the 4th highest cap hit on the team this year. They are going to allow him to earn his money. You may not like it, but it’s going to happen. But Odeyingbo’s situation is complicated. He wasn’t productive last year, and this year he is coming in rehabbing his Achilles tendon. Most players aren’t the same players they were before the injury, at least for a year, and if Odeyingbo is less of what he was last year, that’s an unplayable player. On top of that, this is Odeyingbo’s second career Achilles tendon tear. Was it the same leg or one in each leg? Nobody in the media can seem to get a straight answer, but regardless, that can’t be a good thing for any player, regardless of which one is true. Booker is young, he’s hungry, and he’s definitely on the upswing. If all things were equal, it feels like a virtual certainty that Booker is the starter and perhaps he will be, but Odeyingbo will get the opportunities in training camp to show that he is far more the player that they thought would be worthy of $17 million per year and not the player that looked like a vet-minimum type player (and hoenstly, that might be an insult to vet-minimum guys). Odeyingbo is looking to rebound, Booker is looking to take a big step forward in year three and cement himself as one of the Bears’ starting Edges and earn himself a second contract in Chicago. The Bears need to squeeze every drop of talent out of their defensive line this year if they want to contend, and it’s going to be critical that the Edge position opposite Sweat gives Chicago some type of production. I think that Booker does earn this job and that Odeyingbo ends up competing with Shemar Turner for the team’s third edge. But that’s something we will have to see play out in August.

title: Chicago Bears 2026 Training Camp Position Breakdown: Linebacker
summary: The Chicago Bears made only one* significant change to their linebacking corps this season, but this group will look much different than the group that played in 2025. Roster Locks Tremaine Edmunds, who was much better than fans want to give him credit for, was cut in a cap-saving move, and the Bears signed Devin […]
full_text: Nov 3, 2024; Glendale, Arizona, USA; Chicago Bears linebacker Jack Sanborn (57) against the Arizona Cardinals at State Farm Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Mark J. Rebilas-Imagn Images | Mark J. Rebilas-Imagn Images The Chicago Bears made only one* significant change to their linebacking corps this season, but this group will look much different than the group that played in 2025. Roster Locks Tremaine Edmunds, who was much better than fans want to give him credit for, was cut in a cap-saving move, and the Bears signed Devin Bush to take his place. Bush got a 3-year, $30 million deal, but his cap hit in 2026 will only be $5.6M. The Bears will slide Bush into the weakside linebacker spot, and his speed and athleticism should be an upgrade. Pro Football Focus had Bush as the only linebacker in 2025 (while in Cheveland) to grade above 80 against the run and in pass coverage. The 28-year-old had a slow start to his career, but he’s really coming into his own. The Bears gave D’Marco Jackson a new 2-year, $7.5M deal, with some playing time incentives, and my guess is they want his speed on the field more this season. Last year, he received the first starts of his pro career, and in those 5 games (4 in the regular season, 1 in the playoffs), he had 37 tackles, 2 tackles for loss, a sack, and an interception, while being named the NFC Defensive Player of the Week for his Week 15 performance. His sample size was obviously smaller (261 regular-season defensive snaps), but PFF had him with an overall grade of 83.8. T.J. Edwards was extended last offseason, but he struggled with injuries before he fractured his fibula in the playoff win over the Packers. He was never the fastest linebacker, instead relying on his smarts to give him an edge, so the Bears need him back at 100%. Luckily, early reports had him doing some stuff at OTAs, so he may be ready when training camp opens. Edwards, who won the Brian Piccolo award for the third straight year, is a team leader both on and off the field, and as long as he’s healthy, he’ll be starting at middle linebacker. My guess is that in some defensive subpackages, it’ll be Bush and Jackson staying on the field while Edwards comes off, but this could be matchup reliant depending on the offense’s personnel and down and distance. A Good Bet To Make It The Bears picked Keyshaun Elliott in the fifth round a year after spending a fourth on linebacker Ruben Hyppolite II, but more on Ruben in the next section. Elliot has good instincts and was an excellent blitzer in college. I can see him as the eventual heir apparent at the Mike, but as a rookie, he’ll need to excel in the third phase to cement his spot on the 53. Roster Bubble/Practice Squad *The Bears did bring fan favorite Jack Sanborn back after he spent a year in Dallas, where he missed 11 games with a groin injury. The soon-to-be 26-year-old signed a one-year league minimum deal, but his experience could give him an edge. “I love it here in Chicago and being part of what [coach] Ben Johnson and [defensive coordinator] Dennis Allen have been building here and the success that they’ve had,” Sanborn told ChicagoBears.com after re-signing with his hometown team. “It’s something I couldn’t pass up, and I’m grateful that I’m able to come back here and help in any way I can.” Tony Fields II played in 45 games (10 starts) from 2021 to 2024 with the Browns, but was injured and waived in ’24 before landing on the Rams practice squad. He didn’t play in 2025 after being cut by the Rams, but in 2026, he made the All-UFL team as a member of the Columbus Aviators. His experience will keep him in the mix for a job. Jon Rhattigan is another veteran special teamer with over 1,200 snaps from 2021 to 2025. Wayne Matthews III is a 2026 UDFA from Michigan State, and at his pro day, he was the only non-lineman to hit 20 reps on the bench press. Hyppolite only saw action in 7 games as a rookie (31 snaps on defense and 82 snaps on special teams) while dealing with a shoulder injury and not being able to crack the active game day roster when healthy. His speed and athleticism will give him an opportunity to shine in the third phase, but if he can’t prove worthy of playing defense, he might be destined for the practice squad. The Bears carried 5 linebackers last year, so how many do you think make it this year?

title: Bengals Ring of Honor voting gets even tougher as Willie Anderson reflects on what the honor truly means
summary: The Cincinnati Bengals have done a remarkable job of celebrating the franchise’s history since launching the Ring of Honor in 2021. Now, with another loaded ballot and a growing list of deserving candidates, one of the organization’s all-time greats believes the process is becoming almost impossible. Former Bengals offensive tackle Willie Anderson recently discussed the […]
full_text: CLEVELAND - NOVEMBER 26: Offensive lineman Willie Anderson #71 of the Cincinnati Bengals on the sideline during a game against the Cleveland Browns at Cleveland Browns Stadium on November 26, 2006 in Cleveland, Ohio. The Bengals defeated the Browns 30-0. (Photo by George Gojkovich/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Cincinnati Bengals have done a remarkable job of celebrating the franchise’s history since launching the Ring of Honor in 2021. Now, with another loaded ballot and a growing list of deserving candidates, one of the organization’s all-time greats believes the process is becoming almost impossible. Former Bengals offensive tackle Willie Anderson recently discussed the evolution of the Ring of Honor, sharing his thoughts on what the recognition has meant to him and why future voting decisions will only become more difficult. “You can’t put everybody in” In putting some thoughts on the team’s recent ceremony to honor their past greats, Anderson acknowledged the difficult position fans now find themselves in each summer. Congratulations to these 2 legends who gave their all to @Bengals . I still wanna use this time to say to our Bengals owners “ Please reconsider next year’s plan of only putting 1 player per year in the Ring of honor! So many men are deserving and we want them to be here to… https://t.co/8hYOSst0hb — Willie Anderson (@BigWillie7179) July 22, 2026 With modern stars such as Geno Atkins, Andrew Whitworth, A.J. Green, Carlos Dunlap and Leon Hall joining an already stacked group of former Bengals legends on the ballot, every vote inevitably leaves worthy candidates on the outside looking in. That’s exactly what Anderson expected. The Bengals have quietly built one of the NFL’s deepest collections of franchise legends. While the organization spent years without formally recognizing many of its greats, the Ring of Honor has helped bridge generations of Bengals football—from the Riverfront Stadium era all the way to today’s contenders. The honor hits differently For Anderson, being inducted into the Bengals Ring of Honor in 2022 remains one of the defining moments of his football career. Despite earning four Pro Bowl selections, three First-Team All-Pro honors and continued Hall of Fame consideration, Anderson emphasized that being celebrated by the organization and fan base carried unique meaning. It’s a recognition that comes directly from the people who watched those careers unfold every Sunday. That perspective helps explain why Anderson understands how emotional the annual vote has become. Unlike league-wide awards or Hall of Fame voting, the Bengals Ring of Honor represents something deeply personal between the franchise and its supporters. This year’s vote showed exactly how difficult it’s becoming On Wednesday, the Bengals announced that Bob Trumpy and James Brooks earned induction into the 2026 Ring of Honor after voting by season ticket members. They will officially be honored during halftime of Cincinnati’s Nov. 1 home game against the Tennessee Titans. Both players were unquestionably deserving. Trumpy remains arguably the greatest tight end in franchise history, while Brooks is one of the most explosive offensive players the Bengals have ever fielded. Yet even after those two names came off the board, several all-time Bengals remain waiting. The major issue with the club’s reluctance to put out a Ring of Honor for so many years is a logjam of deserving players having to bide their time long after their great careers ended. It has quietly forced the team to add multiple players per year (ranging from two to four, depending on the year), dimming the exclusivity aspect of a team Hall of Fame. In the unfortunate cases with Trumpy, Paul Brown and Ken Riley, their inductions were posthumous. Had the team engaged in this great endeavor earlier on, at least some of these great Bengals figures would have been able to be present to see their careers come full circle. And, while there are many more deserving names waiting, the franchise recently announced that beginning in 2027, only one individual will be inducted each year instead of two, making future ballots even more competitive. That appears to be the qualm Anderson has with the process. A good problem to have For much of the Bengals’ early history, conversations centered around why so many franchise legends weren’t receiving enough recognition. Today, the discussion has shifted—even with the issues of a late start to a Ring of Honor. Instead of wondering whether the Bengals have enough worthy candidates, fans are debating which deserving legend should go first. That’s a testament to both the organization’s rich history and the success of the Ring of Honor itself. As Willie Anderson noted, there simply isn’t enough room for everyone at once—and that’s perhaps the strongest indication yet that the Bengals have built a legacy worth celebrating for generations to come.

title: James Brooks and Bob Trumpy elected for Bengals Ring of Honor
summary: Cincinnati Bengals season ticket holders apparently have long memories, as they have just elected tight end Bob Trumpy and running back James Brooks to be the latest members of the team’s Ring of Honor. As Geoff Hobson wrote in his article on their selections on Bengals.com, Trumpy was selected in the 12th round of the […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PA - DECEMBER 2: Running back James Brooks #21 of the Cincinnati Bengals runs with the football against the Pittsburgh Steelers during a game at Three Rivers Stadium on December 2, 1990 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. The Bengals defeated the Steelers 16-12. (Photo by George Gojkovich/Getty Images) | Getty Images Cincinnati Bengals season ticket holders apparently have long memories, as they have just elected tight end Bob Trumpy and running back James Brooks to be the latest members of the team’s Ring of Honor. James Brooks and Bob Trumpy are this year's Ring of Honor inductees! 🔗: https://t.co/2JTaZ8W564 pic.twitter.com/HduibqhPjm — Cincinnati Bengals (@Bengals) July 22, 2026 As Geoff Hobson wrote in his article on their selections on Bengals.com , Trumpy was selected in the 12th round of the 1968 Draft, which also happened to be the Bengals’ inaugural season. He was only 215 pounds, but he made the most of his frame with his tremendous receiving ability, grabbing 216 passes in his first six seasons. “He was a top-level player,” Bengals owner Mike Brown said of Trumpy as reported in Hobson’s article. “He had a long stride. He had good hands. Because the safeties couldn’t stay with him, he became a productive downfield threat for us.” Sadly, Trumpy passed away last November at the age of 80, though his memory will continue to live on. Brooks, meanwhile, was acquired from the San Diego Chargers in 1984 via trade. Though only 5’ 10” and 180 pounds, he put up the fifth most rushing yards and fifth most receiving yards of any NFL running back for Cincinnati in the eight seasons that followed. The running back was also fearless in his pass blocking. “He didn’t care how big the pass rusher was,” said Brown. “He went right into him and popped him.” You can read more about both Bengals legends and watch high-quality videos of their careers here in Hobson’s article.

title: Bengals Film Room: Jack Endries can make an impact in Year 1
