title: Answering Dan Hoard’s 5 questions entering Bengals Training Camp 2026
summary: Bengals Training Camp is a week away from getting underway on the Kettering Health Practice Fields behind Paycor Stadium. Storylines abound, and there are many questions going into camp and about the Bengals’ 2026 season. For the second straight season, the Voice of the Bengals, Dan Hoard, released an episode of the Bengals Booth Podcast […]
full_text: Oct 16, 2025; Cincinnati, Ohio, USA; Cincinnati Bengals center Ted Karras (64) reacts after Cincinnati defeated the Pittsburgh Steelers on a late-game field goal by placekicker Evan McPherson (2) (not pictured) during the fourth quarter at Paycor Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Katie Stratman-Imagn Images | Katie Stratman-Imagn Images Bengals Training Camp is a week away from getting underway on the Kettering Health Practice Fields behind Paycor Stadium. Storylines abound, and there are many questions going into camp and about the Bengals’ 2026 season. For the second straight season, the Voice of the Bengals, Dan Hoard, released an episode of the Bengals Booth Podcast where he asked five identical questions to seven Bengals beat writers as we get ready for the grind of Training Camp. Richard Skinner (retired Local12 columnist), James Rapien (host of First Word on The Crown, host of Enter the Jungle on Cincinnati Bengals Talk, publisher/writer for All Bengals at Sports Illustrated), Mike Petraglia (columnist for CLNS Media), Jay Morrison (writer for All Bengals and Sports Illustrated), Paul Dehner Jr. (columnist for The Athletic, host of The Growler Podcast), Kelsey Conway (writer for the Cincinnati Enquirer), and Ben Baby (writer for ESPN.com) all joined Dan Hoard on the latest Bengals Booth Podcast episode to share their answers to Dan’s five questions. After all seven members of the beat shared their answers, Dan shared his own. Now, I’m giving you my answers to Dan’s questions. You can listen to this full episode of the Bengals Booth Podcast below. View Link 1. What is your biggest question going into Training Camp? I actually have three big storylines going into Bengals Training Camp this year. First, how good is the Bengals’ interior offensive line? Orlando Brown Jr. and Amarius Mims are rock solid at the tackles, but what about the inside of the Bengals’ offensive line? Can Dylan Fairchild build on a solid rookie season? Will Ted Karras still be that rock-solid guy at center in his age-33 season? Is Dalton Risner the long-term answer at right guard? It’s going to be fascinating to see these three go up against a completely remade Bengals’ interior defensive line, with the likes of Dexter Lawrence, Jonathan Allen, B.J. Hill, and the second wave of T.J. Slaton, Kris Jenkins Jr., and McKinnley Jackson. Iron sharpens iron, and that will hopefully be the case for the Bengals’ interior offensive line and the Bengals’ defensive line in Training Camp. Second, who is this team’s WR3? Is Andrei Ioisvas going to break out like we kept hearing that he could in each of the last two seasons? What’s Colbie Young’s role going to be? Depth is thin behind Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins. Sure, there are some fun pieces in Charlie Jones and Mitchell Tinsley. But who steps up behind Chase and Higgins is a major question. Third, are the Bengals’ edge rushers going to be a difference-maker on this team? If they are, even after Trey Hendrickson left in free agency this offseason, that would be a major accomplishment. But with Boye Mafe, Myles Murphy, Shemar Stewart, and Cassius Howell in the fold, there is an infusion of talent at a position that’s a huge value and difference-maker in the NFL. Is Stewart going to rewrite an early narrative on his career? Is Mafe entering the prime of his career? Does Murphy build on a strong second half last year? What’s Howell’s role going to be? The edge rushers on this team are fascinating because they’re not getting a lot of attention, but they could. 2. Who is this year’s breakout player? I so wanted to go Jack Endries for this one because he’s, low-key, my favorite draft pick on the Bengals this season. But I’ll save him for another question. For this year’s breakout, I’m going Boye Mafe. Look at who Mafe played with on the Seattle Seahawks’ defense last year, a defense that led the Seahawks to the Super Bowl LX title. If you’re wondering why Mafe’s numbers were down in 2025, that’s why. But it was his ability to pressure the quarterback that impacted Leonard Williams, Uchenna Nwosu, DeMarcus Lawrence, Byron Murphy II, and Jarran Reed and all of their abilities to finish at the quarterback. Now in Cincinnati, Mafe has a greater chance to have bigger numbers this season. While the Bengals’ defensive line is retooled on paper, we still haven’t seen it on the field yet. We know what Mafe can do, and he’s only three seasons removed from a nine-sack season. We saw how great Trey Hendrickson became in his five seasons with the Bengals, and his career took off after signing with them in free agency. Maybe Mafe will have a similar trajectory. 3. Who is this year’s Mitchell Tinsley? Jack Endries. I’m a big fan of the Bengals’ seventh-round pick. He had a really good college career at both California and Texas, and he’s coming in with a chip on his shoulder. The sure-handed pass-catcher could be an asset to the Bengals in short-yardage situations, the red zone, goal-to-go scenarios, and even in between the 40s where a conversion could nullify having to make a decision on whether to punt, go for it, or kick a long field goal. 4. The Bengals win the AFC North if… what? Well, first of all, they need to sweep the Browns. Seriously. Myles Garrett isn’t even in Cleveland anymore. But I’ll echo something Paul Dehner Jr. said, and that’s this Bengals’ offense needs to come out swinging against their division rivals. Remember 2021, when the Bengals swept both the Steelers and Ravens? The Bengals put up 41 points in both games against the Ravens and once against the Steelers. Joe Burrow threw for 941 yards in two games against the Ravens, and Ja’Marr Chase had 326 receiving yards in those two games. Can the Bengals counter the counters the Ravens, Steelers, and Browns showed over the last four seasons? I want to see the Bengals’ offense just come out and unleash an aerial attack that decimates all three teams, whether at home or on the road. Yeah, the Bengals may be constructed differently than the other three teams in the AFC North. But in those division games, screw that. Play your game, and make them beat you. 5. Give a sizzling hot take about the 2026 Bengals I hope you’re ready for this one. For clarity, I don’t 100% believe this will happen. But the point of a hot take, at least in my opinion, is to predict something that could happen but you may not necessarily believe will. This is a two-part hot take. Here goes. The Bengals will HOST the AFC Championship Game against the Pittsburgh Steelers. What an environment that would be if it happens: A night game in The Jungle against the Steelers, with a trip to the Super Bowl on the line. But wait, let’s add something to this. Part two is that Joe Flacco will have to come in for a significant play or drive in the fourth quarter because of something that happens to Joe Burrow. Whether it be a stinger, cramps, or being evaluated for a concussion, Flacco will have to come in for a play or drive, or a half, and I believe he will deliver. Can you imagine if that happens?

title: Browns roster’s fast path to youth: How’d they get there?
summary: The Cleveland Browns have plenty of new talent on this year’s roster. Players have been signed to other teams, while some just weren’t invited back. GM Andrew Berry did a great job bringing in capable bodies and getting rid of the athletes who weren’t getting the job done. And after losing 26 games in the […]
full_text: CINCINNATI, OH - JANUARY 04: Cleveland Browns defensive end Adin Huntington (98) before the game against the Cleveland Browns and the Cincinnati Bengals on January 4, 2026, at Paycor Stadium in Cincinnati, OH. (Photo by Ian Johnson/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Cleveland Browns have plenty of new talent on this year’s roster. Players have been signed to other teams , while some just weren’t invited back. GM Andrew Berry did a great job bringing in capable bodies and getting rid of the athletes who weren’t getting the job done. And after losing 26 games in the past two seasons, a lot of changes and alterations had to be accomplished. RELATED: BROWNS YOUNG ROSTER RANKED TOP-5 Berry’s drafted players from 2025 yielded quite a few new guys who have not only stuck on the roster, but have become starters who have produced. The hope is that the 2026 draft class can do the same. Don’t look now, but the Browns have one of the youngest rosters in the league. Currently, Cleveland has the NFL’s fourth-youngest team . The reason? It can’t be because of free agency. These guys are usually players who have completed their rookie contract after three-or-four-year stints, and the club that drafted them no longer wants their services. Or does not desire to pay out for a huge second contract. The reason is because of the past four drafts. Berry has whiffed on quite a few players in his first three drafts, but has learned from his mistakes and made much better choices. Currently, three players are just 21 years old , and 11 are 22 years old. Another 27 roster members are either 23 or 24. There are only five players who are 30+, with the new fullback, Michael Burton , being s the senior member of the roster at age 35. This is a very young ballclub. Some may point to the fact that it makes this squad inexperienced and prone to mistakes. Which is true. Sometimes. The New England Patriots went from 4-13-0 to 13-4-0 in one year, and they are the NFL’s youngest team. So, there goes that statement stating youth cannot win games. Young talent is always an important aspect for several reasons. Not only are some players instant starters, but the developmental stage is imperative for every roster, especially for depth. A male is at his athletic peak at age 26. And teams want to remain in that range. Let’s examine the past four drafts and examine how many drafted players remain on the current roster: 2026: 10 players selected Still on roster (10 of 10) 2025: 7 players selected Still on roster (7 of 7): DT Mason Graham LB Carson Schwesinger RB Quinshon Judkins TE Harold Fannin QB Dillon Gabriel RB Dylan Sampson QB Shedeur Sanders 2024: 6 players selected Still on roster (5 of 6): DT Mike Hall OG Zak Zinter WR Jamari Thrash LB Bookie Watson CB Myles Harden 2023: 7 players selected Still on roster (4 of 7): WR Ced Tillman OT Dawand Jones DE Isaiah McGuire C Luke Wypler Undrafted rookies signed by Browns who made the roster (all four years) S Ronnie Hickman WR Isaiah Bond DE Adin Huntington S Donovan McMillon LB Easton Mascarenas-Arnold WR Gage Larvadain S Chris Edmonds RB Ahmani Marshall LB Winston Reid WR Luke Floriea That means 26 drafted players from the past four draft classes remain on the current roster. Now, that’s before training camp begins. But that number is 49.06% of the 53-man final roster. Seven of the undrafted rookies who have only played for Cleveland made the final roster as well. That calculates to 33 players on the main roster who remain in their 20s, or 62.26% of the roster. This is a promising young core not only for the upcoming 2026 season, but also the foundation for the Browns for years to come. title: Browns offseason: 5 offseason moves to be positive about
summary: The Cleveland Browns have been mostly a disappointment for the better part of the past 25 years. The franchise has made the playoffs just three times and won just one postseason game since returning to the NFL in 1999. The Browns have had 19 seasons with double-digit losses, posted just the second 0-16 season in […]
full_text: Defensive coordinator Mike Rutenberg coaches at the Browns OTA camp in Berea on May 20, 2026. | Lisa Scalfaro / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images The Cleveland Browns have been mostly a disappointment for the better part of the past 25 years. The franchise has made the playoffs just three times and won just one postseason game since returning to the NFL in 1999. The Browns have had 19 seasons with double-digit losses, posted just the second 0-16 season in league history, and had so many starting quarterbacks and head coaches that it can be hard to remember them at times. This season may be another rough one with a young team led by a first-time head coach and still searching for a quarterback. If the oddsmakers are correct , and they generally are, the 2026 season could bring the number of double-digit losses to an even 20. But there will be plenty of time in the fall to talk about frustrating losses, bad quarterback play, and puzzling coaching decisions. The summer is a time for optimism as training camp brings exciting new players and a renewed hope that this year it may be different. In that spirit, here are five positives from the offseason that should fill the hearts of even the grinchiest Browns fan with a little bit of happiness. The approach to the 2026 NFL Draft The Browns needed to do something about an underperforming wide receiver room, and general manager Andrew Berry wasted no time in selecting KC Concepcion and Denzel Boston. The situation was the same for an aging and injured offensive line, so welcome to Cleveland, Spencer Fano, Austin Barber, and Parker Brailsford. Will all the moves pan out? The history of the NFL says probably not. But Berry recognized the need and used the draft to tackle the problem, so, for now, that is good enough to make the list. The Young Core The new draft class joins running back Quinshon Judkins, defensive tackle Mason Graham, linebacker Carson Schwesinger, and tight end Harold Fannin Jr. from the productive 2025 class to give the Browns a promising foundation of young players to build on. If Concepcion, Boston and Fano are anywhere as good as those second-year players, the Browns should be set up nicely once they finally fix the quarterback situation. (Hopefully, as soon as 2027, because it won’t be this year.) Insisting on Jared Verse The decision to trade defensive end Myles Garrett was understandable, even if it was still disappointing. But insisting that the Los Angeles Rams include Verse in the trade takes some of the sting out, as the Browns will see an immediate return this fall. Verse may not be a force multiplier like Garrett – no one in the NFL is – but adding the 2024 NFL Defensive Rookie of the Year and a player with 99 quarterback pressures in two seasons is something that several teams would have liked to do in the offseason. Hiring Mike Rutenberg as DC Defensive coordinator Jim Schwartz packed up his playbook and went home after the Browns made the correct choice to bypass him for the head coaching role. In his place steps Rutenberg, who will use more zone blitzes to pressure the quarterback , and with the addition of Emmanuel McNeil-Warren, more three-safety looks to keep opposing offenses guessing. Not making the QB situation worse There is no debating that the Browns have the worst quarterback room in the NFL . But as bad as it will be, it could have been worse if Berry had made the mistake of bringing in an aging veteran like Kirk Cousins or Geno Smith, a reclamation project like Justin Fields or Anthony Richardson, or signing a free agent like Malik Willis. None of those players, or any of the other quarterbacks who were available for very obvious reasons, were going to help or be the long-term answer the team needs. It is going to be ugly at times; what else is new, but the Browns need to take their lumps for one more season and then approach the quarterback position in the 2027 NFL Draft. What do you say, Browns fans? Are these true positives or fool’s gold? Have your say in the comments!

title: Origins of Cleveland Browns training camps
summary: Training camp. Why is it called training camp? The reason is to get players back in shape: to “train” their bodies. So, they lived a full life away from the game and ate what they wanted. Back in the day, players and coaches had offseason jobs. When Vince Lombardi was the offensive coordinator with the […]
full_text: A view of the Cleveland Browns 'Brownie the Elf' logo during rookie mini camp at CrossCountry Mortgage Campus (Photo by Nick Cammett/Diamond Images via Getty Images) | Diamond Images/Getty Images Training camp. Why is it called training camp? The reason is to get players back in shape: to “train” their bodies. So, they lived a full life away from the game and ate what they wanted. Back in the day, players and coaches had offseason jobs. When Vince Lombardi was the offensive coordinator with the New York Football Giants, he worked as an executive in a New York bank. He almost remained there. RELATED: ROOKIE AND VETERAN REPORT DATES QB Y.A.Tittle had an insurance business. Even though he is no longer with us, his agency is still going strong. Another quarterback, Frank Ryan of the Cleveland Browns, worked as an assistant professor teaching advanced math at Case Western Reserve University. Roger Staubach sold real estate. Cleveland’s own Jim Brown became a marketing representative for Pepsi-Cola and was an actor in movies. Lou “the Toe” Groza sold insurance. The reason they had desirable jobs was the fact that pro football paid better than most occupations during the season, but did not carry an athlete for all 12 months. Both the Green Bay Packers and Decatur Staleys (later renamed the Chicago Bears) began as company teams. The allure to play for one of these two clubs was that guys could play football and get paid, and after the season was over were hired to work in the plant. Today, player contracts contain workout bonuses. Mostly, athletes will work out during the offseason, and so when they show up for training camp, they are already in shape. Not all, of course, but the percentages are pretty high. If a player spent his offseason working for his father’s tire store, most likely he showed up in shape and was already used to the humidity and heat. If he was a substitute school teacher, chances are he needed to be pushed, and that is what training camp did. The Browns are set to open training camp at the Browns Training Facility in Berea, Ohio on July 22 for rookies and July 28 for the veterans. If you haven’t seen this magnificent complex, it is quite a gem for the players and coaches. Having such a nice place for training camp wasn’t always the case. In fact, players were isolated from the rest of the universe, including their families. In the past, camp was held at a college campus that did not have any students yet, being the summer months. Friends, wives, relatives, church members, and neighbors were only able to come out on certain days and watch practices or able to visit with their player or coach. The remainder of the days of the training camp calendar were reserved for the Browns coaching staff. The remoteness allowed the players to do two things: concentrate on football, and make the final roster. For the longest time, every NFL club found a college campus for training camp. And it was usually the small to medium colleges. Each school had a football team, so there were several practice fields readily available, plus dorm rooms for players and coaches, rooms for meetings, a cafeteria for meals, an area for nutritionists and medical, saunas/cold baths, showers, weight rooms, running track, and the atmosphere was perfect for isolation without any distractions or the comforts of home. Players were basically stuck for weeks on end in college dorm rooms. Up until 1992, the Browns opened training camp somewhere else. From their inception in 1946 up until 1991, Cleveland held training camp at area colleges and universities. Browns training camp locations : 1946-1951: Bowling Green State University (Bowling Green, Ohio) 1952-1974: Hiram College (Hiram, Ohio) 1975-1981: Kent State University (Kent, Ohio) 1982-1991: Lakeland Community College (Kirkland, Ohio) 1992-1995, 1999-present: Browns Training Facility (Berea, Ohio) In the case of the Cleveland Browns being formed, the process began in 1945. The All-America Football Conference (AAFC) was a new pro football league that would become an NFL-rival league. It awarded a franchise to Mickey McBride, who owned several taxi cab companies in Cleveland. He decided to place his team in the City of Cleveland. At the same time, the Cleveland Rams of the NFL were still based in Cleveland. Their owner, Dan Reeves, had for years wanted to relocate the Rams to Los Angeles, but the other NFL owners voted him down each time because of the travel costs. Beginning in 1946, cross-country air travel was now available, and when Reeves saw a rival team moving in, the NFL owners voted to allow him to relocate to Southern California. Here is a capsule of each Browns training camp site: United States Military Bases Paul Brown was a lieutenant in the U.S. Navy. In his last season as a head coach, he had guided Ohio State to a National Championship. His job was waiting for him. McBride approached Brown about the AAFC Cleveland head coaching position. What intrigued Brown was the fact that he could run his own ship. Players didn’t have to worry about finals, studying, or the rigors of campus life. They could concentrate solely on the game. Coach Brown was still in the Navy drawing a paycheck when he accepted the AAFC Cleveland head coaching position. At the same time, his pro football club was in its infancy without any players, front office, assistant coaches, equipment, colors, uniforms, or even a team name. And he was being paid for that, too. Since Coach Brown had coached at Massillon (Ohio) High School, Ohio State University (OSU), and the Great Lakes Navy team that played major college teams, he knew of his own former players. Plus, he had the knowledge of every player that his teams had played against and what their skill levels were. This was a huge advantage; not to mention the fact that he was an officer in the military and had access to information of former NFL players who had to leave their teams and enter the war effort. Plus, there were scores of former college players that would still be playing if it wasn’t for being inserted into the war effort. Coach Brown knew where each athlete was currently stationed, which branch they were in, and how to contact them. Coach Brown compiled a list of targeted athletes. Unknown to most, a lot of Browns’ players were signed while still in the military (just as Brown had been) and paid monthly retainers with AAFC Cleveland. Coach Brown sent out in the standard military mail to prospective players a personal letter, an offer of $250 per month until the war ceased, a signing bonus of $2,500, and when they arrived at Cleveland’s training camp, a $7,500 salary to play professional football with the new AAFC Cleveland ballclub. Coach Brown contacted Otto Graham, who was stationed in the Navy’s V-12 flying program. OT Lou Groza and OG Lin Houston had played for the freshman team while Brown was head coach at OSU. The following year, both players enlisted and missed their final three college years and were now in the Philippines when they were contacted. After signing, Groza, also a kicker, was sent two footballs in the mail to begin practicing. WR Dante Lavelli had fought in the Battle of the Bulge and was serving in the 28 th Infantry Division when he signed. WR Mac Speedie was seen by Coach Brown when he was playing for a Marine Corps team. DB Al Akins was serving in the Pacific when he got Brown’s letter. Coach found OG Ed Ulinski, whom he remembered playing at Marshall University and now was in the Air Force. In all, 26 of the players signed to the 36-man roster had played in the NFL or had been drafted by an NFL club before enlisting in the military. Each player signed while still in the military was given detailed exercise instructions with daily running routine procedures to follow. This essentially became the Browns’ first unofficial training camp. Bowling Green State University: 1946-1951 Once World War II was over and the Browns’ coaches and players could finally get…

title: Cowboys news: Diving into the competition at offensive tackle
summary: Cowboys Depth Chart: Training camp competition awaits at offensive tackle – Nick Harris, Fort Worth Star-Telegram There are some things to work out at offensive tackle. Safe (4) Tyler Guyton, Terence Steele, Nate Thomas, Drew Shelton While there will be competition at left tackle and questions still exist around the long-term stability at right tackle, […]
full_text: ARLINGTON, TX - SEPTEMBER 14: Tyler Guyton #60 of the Dallas Cowboys runs across the field during an NFL football game against the New York Giants at AT&T Field on September 14, 2025 in Arlington, Texas. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images Cowboys Depth Chart: Training camp competition awaits at offensive tackle – Nick Harris, Fort Worth Star-Telegram There are some things to work out at offensive tackle. Safe (4) Tyler Guyton, Terence Steele, Nate Thomas, Drew Shelton While there will be competition at left tackle and questions still exist around the long-term stability at right tackle, the 53-man roster spots are safe at the top of the room. Tyler Guyton is the one with the biggest microscope on him going into training camp. The 2024 first-round pick has yet to put together a fully healthy training camp, much less a fully healthy season. After head coach Brian Schottenheimer said during OTAs that Guyton’s starting job is up for grabs , the need for progression is bigger than it has ever been for the Oklahoma product. Through two seasons, Guyton has allowed 57 quarterback pressures and eight sacks. On the other side, Terence Steele should be able to hold down his starting job at right tackle because of his strong run blocking ability. However, lapses exist in his pass protection, as he’s given up 93 quarterback pressures and 15 sacks over the past two seasons. He’s been a staple of durability since tearing his ACL in 2022, though, as he’s started every game over the past three seasons. At left tackle, 2024 seventh-round pick Nate Thomas is Guyton’s biggest threat for the starting job. After being moved from guard to tackle before training camp last season, Thomas quickly ascended up the depth chart. He is now in position to be the starting left tackle, at best, or the backup swing tackle with a strong training camp. The staff’s confidence in Thomas didn’t quite translate onto the field; across 219 pass block snaps last season, Thomas allowed 23 pressures and three sacks. The dark horse in the room is fourth-round rookie Drew Shelton . In a draft class that had an overflowing bucket of right tackle talent, the Cowboys took a day-three swing on Shelton, who primarily played left tackle at Penn State. Across 356 pass block snaps as a senior, Shelton allowed just 18 pressures and one sack. With a lack of confidence at the top of the depth chart, a path exists for Shelton to make a big impact as a rookie with a strong training camp. Myth Busting Season: 3 Dallas Cowboys storylines that training camp will reveal more about, including Caleb Downs’ role – Mauricio Rodriguez, AtoZ Sports These will certainly be some interesting things to watch. Dallas Cowboys training camp is days away, and with it comes the annual opportunity to separate fact from fiction. Every offseason, Cowboys coaches drop hints about how they plan to use certain players, and every year, some of those hints turn out to be a whole bunch of nothing. Or at the very least, nothing compared to what Cowboys fans and media make them out to be. I’m talking about when the Cowboys hinted fullback Hunter Huepke would evolve into a tight end. Or when wide receiver KaVontae Turpin was supposed to take running back snaps. And one of my favorites: when Tony Pollard was going to line up as a slot receiver. All of those storylines fizzled. But there have been many others that turn out to be true. Today, we’re looking at three storylines that I wonder if they’re true or myth. Let’s begin with the biggest name of the offseason… George Pickens as a slot receiver One of the biggest offseason talking points surrounding the Cowboys offense has been the plan to move Pickens around the formation. Cowboys head coach Brian Schottenheimer said Pickens “does not like” to stay in one spot and wants to be moved around. Last year, offensive coordinator Klayton Adams admitted the coaching staff didn’t realize how dynamic Pickens could be with the ball in his hands until CeeDee Lamb went down with an injury last season. The numbers paint a clear picture of just how different this would be. Among qualifying wide receivers, Pickens had the second-lowest percentage of snaps in the slot across the NFL, according to Pro Football Focus. Moving him inside would represent a dramatic shift in how Dallas deploys its top pass catcher. If Pickens isn’t lining up inside during training camp practices, expectations should come back down to earth quickly—but it wouldn’t be enough to lower the Pickens hype. No.4) What are you hoping to see in Parker’s defense? – Tommy Yarrish, DallasCowboys.com What will the defense in Dallas look like under Christian Parker in his first year running the show? Tommy: Turnovers. Brian Schottenheimer has consistently harped on how frustrated he was in his team’s turnover ratio last season, where the Cowboys were -9, tied for third-worst in the league with 21 turnovers compared to 12 takeaways. Of course, most of Schottenheimer’s frustration likely comes as the play caller and with the offense, as 21 turnovers isn’t ideal for any good offense. That said, with a good offense you need to give them more possessions. Getting turnovers is the best way to do that and set up Dak Prescott and company in a positive position to go and put points on the board. That is what will go a long way to helping the Cowboys win more games. Of course, you aren’t going to get a turnover on every play and need to be a solid defense in general, but quick changes of possession caused by turnovers turn games on their heads. If those turnovers are able to come from the secondary and through interceptions, that’s a big testament to what Parker has been able to do with the unit that dealt with a plethora of injuries and only had six interceptions total last season. Dallas Cowboys pre-training camp roster projection: Notable cuts, darkhorse candidates and more – Joseph Hoyt, Dallas Morning News Diving into what the Cowboys roster could look like in 2026. Quarterback (3) Dak Prescott, Sam Howell, Joe Milton III Notable cuts: N/A Briefly: Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescott would probably urge you not to issue causation due to correlation, but still, there is a trend worth noting when it comes to his career. Since 2020, he’s alternated between playing a full season and missing a significant amount of time. This coming season, he’s trying to string together healthy seasons in back-to-back years for the first time since 2019. That makes having a backup quarterback position important. The Cowboys brought in Sam Howell to compete with the raw but talented Joe Milton . Howell has a full season’s worth of starting experience. Could that be enough to win the battle? Wild card: If the Cowboys see enough from Howell or Milton, could they run the risk of having just two quarterbacks on the active roster? It’s something they did a season ago with Milton and former quarterback Will Grier, who spent all of last season on the practice squad but recently announced his retirement. Running back (5) Javonte Williams, Jaydon Blue, Phil Mafah, Hunter Luepke, Malik Davis Notable cuts: Israel Abanikanda, Dominic Richardson Briefly: The Cowboys know who their starting running back will be. That’s why you won’t see much of Javonte Williams during preseason. They’ve also been adamant about their optimism for second-year running backs Jaydon Blue and Phil Mafah. They expect both to take a big step this season. That probably places Malik Davis on the roster bubble. In this case, however, we keep Davis. He’s someone the Cowboys know they can trust on special teams. He’s the team’s starting personal protector on punt coverage. Will that be enough for him to make the roster? Wild card: The Cowboys signed Hunter Luepke to an extension last season, but he was used on just over 20% of the offensive snaps last season. Could he be on the bubble, especially if the emergence of a run-blocking tight end like Brevyn Spann-Ford continues in camp? Daily…

title: This new Cowboy will be an important part of training camp
summary: It has often been said that there is nobody more popular on a football team than the backup quarterback. That may not be so literally true regarding the Dallas Cowboys of now. Dak Prescott remains in place at one of the more polarizing positions in sports, but it does feel like for the most part […]
full_text: Jun 16, 2026; Dallas, TX, USA; Dallas Cowboys quarterback Sam Howell (16) and wide receiver Marquez Valdes-Scantling (11) go through a drill during practice at the Ford Center at the Star Training Facility in Frisco, Texas. Mandatory Credit: Chris Jones-Imagn Images | Chris Jones-Imagn Images It has often been said that there is nobody more popular on a football team than the backup quarterback. That may not be so literally true regarding the Dallas Cowboys of now. Dak Prescott remains in place at one of the more polarizing positions in sports, but it does feel like for the most part football fans in general acknowledge that he is one of the better players of his position. Postseason success sure wouldn’t hurt, though. While Dak may not be under duress from a backup in his own building, the role of QB2 remains critical nonetheless. Regarding Dak specifically, it is important to remember that he has a bit of an injury concern in recent years and so being prepared for that hypothetical is never a bad idea. This is where training camp is going to help mine an answer. Sam Howell is going to be very important throughout camp Is Joe Milton the backup quarterback on this team right now? If you answered yes, did you do so confidently? There is a lot to like about Milton and his athletic profile. There is zero doubt that he is an intriguing prospect and someone who may be molded into a proper NFL signal-caller. He can also throw it a mile. Unfortunately, Milton doesn’t exactly have a ton of NFL experience. He does have that within the Cowboys as he was the team’s primary backup last year, but the front office and coaching staff didn’t bring in Sam Howell for no reason at all. This is the case because Howell has legitimate NFL starts to his name. In fact, Howell has an entire season’s worth of starts on his resumé. Howell was Washington’s starter across the entire 2023 season. He even earned a place in Cowboys lore that season as it was his interception which DaRon Bland returned for a touchdown to set the record for most in a single season, a feat that Jim Nantz brilliantly called on Thanksgiving Day. Obviously a season where the Commanders won four games and Howell etched his name in Cowboys history with an interception of all things isn’t worth throwing a party over; however, Howell fits the archetype of backup quarterback. He is still young, he’ll be 26 soon, and has faced the fire that playing quarterback in the NFL commands. Simply put, he has lived this job in ways that Joe Milton hasn’t. That was obviously interesting enough to the team for them to bring him in. Given that the Cowboys have such an obvious answer at starting quarterback, the pressure throughout camp is going to be on the backup position, again, especially if we acknowledge Prescott’s medical history. What’s more is that Prescott may earn himself a veteran day or two, and on those days the primary backup is even going to get to work with the starters. The position is valuable and whoever holds it has to be a proper caretaker. Modern NFL rules are such that it is practical for teams to carry three quarterbacks on their roster, so nobody is in danger of losing their actual spot on the team. But it is imperative for the Cowboys to find and establish an answer regarding who their second in command will be. While we have you here, go ahead and vote in our latest poll concerning RB Javonte Williams.

title: Cowboys 2026 roster rundown: OL DJ Wingfield
summary: There will be plenty of undrafted rookies in the Cowboys’ 2026 training camp, but few with a story like DJ Wingfield’s. After missing all of 2025 over an eligibility issue, Wingfield hopes to keep his NFL dreams alive despite the ugly end of his college career. Background Years in NFL: 0Acquired by: UDFA (2026) After graduating from […]
full_text: COLUMBUS, OH - NOVEMBER 09: Purdue Boilermakers offensive lineman DJ Wingfield (55) lines up during the game against the Purdue Boilermakers and the Ohio State Buckeyes on November 9, 2024, at Ohio Stadium in Columbus, OH. (Photo by Ian Johnson/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images There will be plenty of undrafted rookies in the Cowboys’ 2026 training camp, but few with a story like DJ Wingfield’s. After missing all of 2025 over an eligibility issue, Wingfield hopes to keep his NFL dreams alive despite the ugly end of his college career. Background Years in NFL: 0 Acquired by: UDFA (2026) After graduating from high school in 2019, Wingfield played for a few years at local community college. He joined the New Mexico Lobos from 2022-2023, playing mostly right guard but a little tackle as well. He then transferred to Purdue for one year, starting all 12 games at guard. In 2025, Wingfield transferred to USC with the promise of a substantive $210k NIL deal. But he didn’t realize that he’d exhausted his college eligibility, and the NCAA denied an appeal to allow him to play for the Trojans. Wingfield sat out for a year, but USC did allow him to participate in their Pro Day last March. It wasn’t enough to get him drafted, but Wingfield signed with Dallas in May after a tryout during their rookie minicamp. Contract Status Years Left: 3 2026 Cap Hit: $885k Given his extended college career and what happened last year, Wingfield is an old rookie at 25. He’ll already be 28 when this rookie deal ends, if he sticks around that long. 2026 Projections Role: Backup OL Roster Chance: 10% USC threw a lot of money Wingfield’s way last year, so there’s reason to be intrigued. The Cowboys’ offensive line is going to be tough to crack, though maybe a little easier now for a guard prospect than a tackle. Dallas had signed veteran Matt Hennessy to likely replace Brock Hoffman as an interior backup, but he’s out for the year now following an offseason neck injury. Even still, Wingfield will have to go through a gauntlet of options to make the roster. T.J. Bass has one reserve spot locked down. After the Hennessy injury, Dallas signed G/C Chris Glaser from the UFL, who also has a little NFL experience from 2023-2024. Then there’s Trevor Keegan, who made the roster last year, plus veteran Nick Leverett who was on last year’s practice squad. Throw in position flex for tackle prospects like Nate Thomas and Ajani Cornelius, and it’s clear Wingfield will have to be one of the biggest surprises of camp to stick around. It can happen, though. Wingfield need only look over at Terence Steele, who nobody saw coming as a UDFA in 2020. Injuries helped Steele get into games, but it was a shockingly good camp that put him in position. Given Wingfield’s unorthodox entry to the NFL, who knows how quickly he might start distinguishing himself from other backup prospects? The Cowboys have a knack for finding talent in unusual places, and Wingfield has a chance to be the next success story for Will McClay’s crew. Steele and other UDFAs have taught us that what happens over the next month is far more important than how you got here. Wingfield will have plenty of competition, and may have to take being on the practice squad as a victory. But given how last year went for him, even still being in the fight is an accomplishment. title: Cowboys countdown to kickoff: Top 100 iconic games – Day 53
summary: It is Day 53 of our 100-day countdown to kickoff. We are looking back at the 100 most iconic games in Dallas Cowboys history. The countdown will leads us right up to the opening game of 2026. Our look back doesn’t depend on just one criteria for our rankings. We take into consideration things like […]
full_text: It is Day 53 of our 100-day countdown to kickoff. We are looking back at the 100 most iconic games in Dallas Cowboys history. The countdown will leads us right up to the opening game of 2026. Our look back doesn’t depend on just one criteria for our rankings. We take into consideration things like how big the game was for the organization, how memorable the game was, games that had unusual events take place, games that are a part of NFL lore, Cowboys firsts, and games where the Cowboys just plain dominated. Variety is the spice of life and we have all different kind of Cowboys games to review. At the bottom, we’ll link each day of the countdown so you can go back and check out any you missed. Let’s kick things off here for Day 53 of our 100-day countdown to kickoff, as we revisit one of the wildest finishes in Cowboys history. Dallas appeared beaten several times against the New York Giants last year, only for Dak Prescott to keep answering and Brandon Aubrey to produce two pressure kicks that turned a likely defeat into overtime victory. Sunday, September 14, 2025 — 1:00 p.m. ET AT&T Stadium, Arlington, Texas Final Score: Dallas Cowboys 40, New York Giants 37 (OT) Desperation was on the menu for Week 2 as both teams hunted for their first win of the 2025 season. Early on, it was all New York. Russell Wilson had the Giants flying high with a 13-3 lead while the Cowboys offense looked stuck in first gear. Prescott finally found the clutch, hitting KaVontae Turpin for a much-needed house call, but Dallas still went into halftime chasing the Giants 13-10. The game began to change after Prescott threw an interception early in the third quarter. New York started at the Dallas 40-yard line but failed on fourth down near the goal line. The Cowboys immediately travelled 90 yards in six plays, with Javonte Williams breaking tackles on a 30-yard touchdown run that gave Dallas its first lead at 17-13. That advantage was only the beginning of the chaos. New York cut the score to 17-16 before Aubrey made a 44-yard field goal. Cam Skattebo’s short touchdown then put the Giants ahead 23-20, but Prescott answered by completing all five of his passes on the next Dallas possession. Miles Sanders finished the drive with a four-yard touchdown run to restore the Cowboys’ lead. The final three minutes became a contest in which neither defense could protect an advantage. Wilson found Wan’Dale Robinson for a touchdown on fourth-and-four, putting New York ahead 30-27 with 2:44 remaining. Prescott responded by taking Dallas 71 yards in less than two minutes, finishing the drive with a touchdown pass to George Pickens near the left pylon. With less than a minute remaining, Dallas led 34-30. However, Wilson quickly responded with two plays. Scrambling into Cowboys territory, he launched a deep pass to Malik Nabers, who caught it between two defenders for a 48-yard touchdown. This move propelled New York back into the lead, with a final score of 37-34, just 33 seconds left. Prescott still refused to let the game end. An 18-yard completion to Jake Ferguson moved the ball to the Giants’ 49-yard line, and Williams gained four more yards on a quick handoff. Dallas then asked Aubrey to attempt a 64-yard field goal with five seconds remaining. Aubrey drove the ball through the uprights as time expired, tying the score at 37 and sending the game into overtime. It was another example of why his range changes how Dallas can manage late-game situations. Neither team scored on its first overtime possession, and Dallas eventually punted for a second time. With the clock approaching two minutes, Wilson attempted another deep pass toward Nabers. Donovan Wilson intercepted it at the Dallas 30-yard line, providing the Cowboys with the defensive play they had been missing throughout the afternoon. Prescott immediately found Pickens for 27 yards, followed by an insanely well executed scramble for 14 more, moving Dallas to the New York 28. Aubrey came onto the field with four seconds remaining and calmly converted a 46-yard field goal, securing the win for the second time that afternoon as the clock struck zero. This game belongs on the countdown because of how many times Dallas appeared to have lost it. The Cowboys surrendered three go-ahead touchdowns during the fourth quarter, gave up 450 passing yards and were seconds away from a tie game. Prescott’s late-game composure, Donovan Wilson’s interception and Aubrey’s extraordinary range allowed them to survive every mistake. #Cowboys vs #Giants 2025 Week 2 The @Brandon_Aubrey Double Pressure Kick Final Score: Dallas Cowboys 40, New York Giants 37 (OT) #DallasCowboys #NFL (📽️: @nfl ) pic.twitter.com/nmzRCsB239 — Mike Poland (@kenfigkowboy) July 21, 2026 Interesting Facts About the Game The 64-yard field goal was the second-longest successful kick of Aubrey’s career. It also made him the first player to convert multiple field goals from at least 64 yards. title: One prediction for training camp, running backs edition
summary: We continue our Dallas Cowboys training camp prediction series. Today we’ll look at one of the units on offense that experienced success in 2025, the running backs. Dallas will carry over the ninth-best rushing attack in terms of yards into 2026, but after a career year from lead back Javonte Williams, 1,201 yards, 11 TDs […]
full_text: Mandatory Credit: Andrew Dieb-Imagn Images | Andrew Dieb-Imagn Images We continue our Dallas Cowboys training camp prediction series. Today we’ll look at one of the units on offense that experienced success in 2025, the running backs. Dallas will carry over the ninth-best rushing attack in terms of yards into 2026, but after a career year from lead back Javonte Williams, 1,201 yards, 11 TDs on 252 carries, some fans are worried that Williams may not be able to keep up the pace. Somebody has to develop behind Williams, not to just to pick up the slack for any kind of drop-off, but also just to spell and complement the lead back. Last year, Cowboys running backs not named Williams rushed for 397 yards and three touchdowns on 95 carries. That means they rushed for a respectable 4.17 yards a carry, but those numbers are hardly inspiring. The candidates for the RB2 position basically come down to Jaydon Blue, Phil Mafah and Malik Davis. Prediction: Phil Mafah will emerge as the best back behind Williams At 6’0”, 234 lbs. Phil Mafah has the physical tools to be able to swipe the second RB spot, as well as the downhill style to complement Williams unlike any other back on the roster. If Mafah can take the reins behind Williams, that not only helps open up the run game and offense but also creates an opportunity for all the other backs on the roster to have more clearly defined roles, which could help what was already an efficient unit in 2025 become even more effective. Mafah only played in one game last year, getting five carries for 18 yards and a touchdown. So he may not look like the guy to jump into the RB2 spot, but we’re going bold with our prediction. Do you agree? Who do you got in the RB2 competition? Let us know in the comments and also vote in our poll below. Vote in our poll for how many rushing yards Javonte Williams will get in 2026.

title: Team captains wanted for Cowboys under Brian Schottenheimer
summary: One of the many changes Brian Schottenheimer brought to the Cowboys that may have gone largely unnoticed is the re-introduction of permanent team captains. Under Mike McCarthy, the Cowboys had a rotating system that allowed dozens of players to serve as captain at least once. In some cases, players that were on the practice squad […]
full_text: Jun 16, 2026; Dallas, TX, USA; Dallas Cowboys head coach Brian Schottenheimer addresses the media before practice at the Ford Center at the Star Training Facility in Frisco, Texas. Mandatory Credit: Chris Jones-Imagn Images | Chris Jones-Imagn Images One of the many changes Brian Schottenheimer brought to the Cowboys that may have gone largely unnoticed is the re-introduction of permanent team captains. Under Mike McCarthy, the Cowboys had a rotating system that allowed dozens of players to serve as captain at least once. In some cases, players that were on the practice squad a week earlier were elevated to captains. McCarthy defended it as a way to promote leadership across the roster, but that approach never quite sat right with the fans. But since last year, the Cowboys are back to a system that features six team captains (two per team unit and each with a permanent “C” patch on their uniforms) and one captain rotating on a weekly basis based on performance in practice and meetings throughout the week. body .sbnu-legacy-content-table td, body .sbnu-legacy-content-table th, body .sbnu-legacy-content-table { border: 1px solid #000 !important; border-collapse: collapse !important; } body .sbnu-legacy-content-table td, body .sbnu-legacy-content-table th { padding: 4px 6px !important; } 2020 – 2024 2025 Team Unit Team Captains Team Captains Offense Rotating system that allowed dozens of players to serve as captain at least once. In some cases, even practice squad call-ups wore the title. Dak Prescott, CeeDee Lamb Defense Osa Odighizuwa, Donovan Wilson Special Teams Brandon Aubrey, CJ Goodwin NFL teams traditionally announce their team captains on or very close to opening weekend. This is usually something that is done without much fanfare, and in past years where the Cowboys had permanent captains, the names were usually chosen from among the team’s most visible players. But this year could be different, as three of last year’s captains, Osa Odighizuwa, Donovan Wilson, and C.J. Goodwin are no longer with the team and have created vacancies. There are a lot of new players on defense. Players like Kenny Clark, Quinnen Williams, Rashan Gary, or Jalen Thompson may not have held the title in Dallas last year, but are significant locker room presences. Kenny Clark was a three-time captain in Green Bay, as was Williams with the Jets. Gary was a captain in Green Bay last year, and Thompson has one star on his “C” patch as well. There were no significant personnel changes on offense, but Tyler Smith and Tyler Booker are increasingly emerging as leaders on the offensive line. And Brian Schottenheimer will also have some ideas about who he wants to see in that leadership role. In a recent press conference , he mentioned the following names (among many others) as young players who stood out in a leadership role in OTAs and minicamp: Donovan Ezeiruaku, DeMarvion Overhown, Shemar James, and Caleb Downs. Former safety Darren Woodson, three-time Super Bowl winner and a member of the Cowboys’ Ring of Honor, recently spoke on the Doin’ Alright podcast about what made the Cowboys successful in the 90s. “You want to win football games, you get them boys up front lined up. They’re big boys, they’ve got some pride in that front seven. That’s when you start to connect.” “We were at our best – as Super Bowl champions – not because of the skill guys, but because our offensive line was the best in the league and our defensive line, we had a seven-man rotation, and they didn’t drop, and they had so much pride in what they were doing. That’s what was connected.” “And they ran the locker room. Don’t let your DBs and wide receivers run the locker room! Your defensive backs and wide receivers run the locker room? You’ve got a problem.” “When your offensive and defensive line are telling everybody ‘Shut up! Get your ass in line.’ ” “That’s when you’ve got something.“ Who would you like to see step up as team captain this year?

title: The one thing the Cowboys are doing differently that no one is talking about
summary: The Dallas Cowboys are doing Dallas Cowboys things this offseason, but lo and behold, many people are convinced that this year is different. The front office is finally acting like a well-behaved organization and keeping a lower profile this offseason compared to previous years. At least that is how some feel, but is that really […]
full_text: The Dallas Cowboys are doing Dallas Cowboys things this offseason, but lo and behold, many people are convinced that this year is different. The front office is finally acting like a well-behaved organization and keeping a lower profile this offseason compared to previous years. At least that is how some feel, but is that really the case? Yesterday, we went down the list one by one and explained how the things this team is notorious for doing in past seasons, they are still doing this offseason. Check out this article for more details. Or, if you want the CliffNotes version, here you go… Contract standoffs – They franchised-tagged George Pickens and never attempted any extension negotiations with him. The opportunity for drama was huge, but it didn’t exist because Pickens decided to just play under his contract. Good on him, but when it comes to the front office, what did they do to deescalate the drama? Nothing. No change. Limited free agent spending – They bought one higher-priced player in Jalen Thompson, but that’s all. They then proceeded to sign a slew of low-cost depth guys to fill voids. When you look at the books, they are still way down in the shallow end of the free agency spending pool. No change. New coaches – Another year, another new defensive coordinator. But this time he’s an unproven guy instead of a former head coach retread. But remember, last year they hired an unproven first-timer on the offensive side in Klayton Adams. That seemed pretty smart, and only further piques our interest in Christian Parker, but comparing the two offseasons? Again, no change. Players returning from injuries – People were hoping that Trevon Diggs, DeMarvion Overshown, and Sam Williams would return to form and be ready to perform at a strong level. They weren’t. Now, those same hopes fall on Shavon Revel Jr., DaRon Bland, and Overshown again. This may or may not work out differently, but again, we find them in a very similar situation. Now that we have run through a lot of the things that felt different but really are not, it is time to finally address what has truly changed and paint a more pleasant picture of optimism heading into the new season. The Joneses have done something different this offseason, but it is not something many people are talking about. The great philosopher J. Wellington Wimpy once said, “I will gladly pay you Tuesday for a hamburger today.” The Cowboys have embraced this pay-for-it-later approach and decided to mortgage their future for extra funds right now. Entering the offseason, the Cowboys were outside the top 20 in allocated money in void years , but in one swift offseason, they climbed to the fourth-highest in the league . The front office restructured several contracts, clearing out cap space and pushing this massive financial liability into future years. They now stand at four times the NFL median, but this is what they feel they have to do to keep up. The Philadelphia Eagles have exploited this practice to the highest degree, with over 10 times the median value, which is absolutely insane. This bookkeeping trick has allowed the Cowboys to acquire and retain more high-priced assets than in previous years. Handling the Pickens franchise tag hit? No problem. Taking on the hefty salaries of Quinnen Williams, Kenny Clark, and Rashan Gary? Bring it on. Tweaking contracts to hang on to solid players who would otherwise be cap casualties, like Terence Steele and Malik Hooker? They have done that as well. The Cowboys decided to hold on to as many pieces as they could to keep the roster stronger, rather than picking and choosing so they can maintain a respectable budget. Make no mistake about it, this is a huge change. Borrowing cap resources from the future to help the team now is a big deal. The front office has done this before, but never to this extent. And it comes with no promises, but at least we can genuinely say they are really trying. This is what is actually different. When you look at this offseason, a lot of what we are seeing is right on brand for the Cowboys’ front office. Many of the things they have done are very similar to those of previous years. It is just that they have enough added resources to appease the natives and keep Cowboys Nation from rioting. From a roster-building standpoint, the team has done quite a lot to improve the product on the field, and now it is in the hands of the new coaches and players to make things work.

title: Predicting rushing yards from Cowboys RB Javonte Williams in 2026
summary: You can almost smell it. Football is right around the corner as the Dallas Cowboys will be heading to Oxnard, California next week to kickoff 2026 training camp. While we have spent a lot of time talking about the Cowboys defense this offseason, the offense is the Cowboys calling card. This is where they shine, […]
full_text: Jun 16, 2026; Dallas, TX, USA; Dallas Cowboys running back Javonte Williams (33) goes through a drill during practice at the Ford Center at the Star Training Facility in Frisco, Texas. Mandatory Credit: Chris Jones-Imagn Images | Chris Jones-Imagn Images You can almost smell it. Football is right around the corner as the Dallas Cowboys will be heading to Oxnard, California next week to kickoff 2026 training camp. While we have spent a lot of time talking about the Cowboys defense this offseason, the offense is the Cowboys calling card. This is where they shine, and one reason for that last year was the play of running back Javonte Williams. Williams had 252 carries for 1,201 rushing yards in 2025, a career best. His previous high, 203 carries for 903 rushing yards, came in his rookie season. Williams is back on a new free agent deal and will be expected to carry the load at running back. So we want to know how you think he follows up last season. We have five choices. Less than 1,000 yards This probably means two things. Either injury has struck, or one of the backups steps up and eats into Williams reps, allowing the Cowboys to rest him some. 1,000 – 1,099 yards This would be a solid follow-up as long as someone else is kicking in from the backup spot. 1,100 – 1,199 yards Another solid number, but also likely that Williams is keeping the bulk of the reps. 1,200 – 1,299 yards Matching last year would put Williams in the conversation for one of the better starting running backs in the NFL. 1,300+ yards If this happens, Williams is having the season of his life with plenty of grinding out the clock in games the team is leading, and/or absolutely no one is giving him any relief from the RB2 spot. title: Cowboys Oxnard training camp roundtable discussion
summary: Every so often, we gather to discuss the latest news about the Dallas Cowboys and seek our writer’s perspective on each headline. Welcome back to the roundtable. This week we have Jess Haynie, Sean Martin, Brian Martin, and for his first Roundtable appearance we have Jorge Guajardo. Which rookie are you most excited to watch in training […]
full_text: Jul 27, 2025; Oxnard, CA, USA; Dallas Cowboys defensive players run drills at training camp at the River Ridge Fields. Mandatory Credit: Kirby Lee-Imagn Images | Kirby Lee-Imagn Images Every so often, we gather to discuss the latest news about the Dallas Cowboys and seek our writer’s perspective on each headline. Welcome back to the roundtable. This week we have Jess Haynie, Sean Martin, Brian Martin, and for his first Roundtable appearance we have Jorge Guajardo. Which rookie are you most excited to watch in training camp this year? Mike: Jaishawn Barham is the rookie I’m most excited to watch because linebacker was one of Dallas’ biggest weaknesses last season and desperately needed an upgrade. Barham is has the size to handle traffic between the tackles, but also the athleticism to chase plays outside and create pressure when sent after the quarterback. Training camp will show how quickly he diagnoses offenses and earns the coaches’ trust, but the opportunity is there for him. Jess: If we’re all being honest, the answer is Caleb Downs. So I’ll go with my next guy, Jaishawn Barham. We’re desperate for stability at inside linebacker, let alone a playmaker. Even if DeMarvion Overshown explodes this year, and his knee doesn’t, we still need one more guy to help make this defense competitive again. Comparisons between Barham and the Eagles’ Zack Baun, given the Christian Parker connection, are also tantalizing. Jorge: The answer is Caleb Downs, but I really want to see Michael Trigg. TE is one of the deepest position groups on this team, and if Brevyn Spann-Ford makes a leap, the path to the 53-man roster gets really tough for everybody behind Spann-Ford, setting up what could be a desperate attempt to make the roster, which, I think, always leads to entertaining and even good football. Trigg is a physical specimen, so seeing him fight and claw for a roster spot could be epic, and could light a fire under the other TEs on the roster as well. Brian: As much as I’m looking forward to seeing what Caleb Downs can do in the ever important nickel/safety role in Christian Parker’s scheme, I’m going to go with the Cowboys other first-round pick, Malachi Lawrence. Dallas’ pass rush was pretty much nonexistent a season ago, but will hopefully be much improved this year with the new, versatile 3-4 scheme and the additions of Rashan Gary and Lawrence. The rookie could play a big role as a pass rush specialist or maybe even earn a starting role. Sean: Kind of an “old man sitting on the porch” answer from me, which believe me doesn’t feel too great on a personal level, but I’ve covered enough Cowboys camps at this point to know that it is a yearly tradition like no other to absolutely lose our minds over a fringe wide receiver that makes some intriguing plays. It is the one position where a huge swarm of fans always have a “pet cat” they swear has to be a roster lock, very few ever are, but the fun and enthusiasm still goes on year after year. For these reasons I’m going with seventh-round pick Anthony Smith, who has the speed to make plenty of social media highlights potentially getting behind a Christian Parker secondary that won’t take too well to giving up big plays, making the back and forth that much more intense. Let’s see what Anthony Smith can do. Name an underrated player you think will shine in Oxnard? Mike: Brevyn Spann-Ford is my underrated player to watch in Oxnard. He was already trending upward last season despite sitting third on the tight end depth chart, and he has a genuine opportunity to overtake Luke Schoonmaker for the number two role. Spann-Ford’s size and catch radius make him an intriguing target. Jess: Training camp seems to always be when CB Caelen Carson shines. The problem is that we haven’t seen it carry into the regular season, either due to injuries or just general inexperience. Now in his third season, and playing under a DB guru in Parker, I’m intrigued to see if many have been too quick to dismiss Carson as a contender this summer. Jorge: For the same reasons Jess believes in Caelen Carson, I’m going to go with Shavon Revel. He has all the tools to be a solid contributor at the NFL level. He finally has a full, injury-free offseason to work on his craft and be mentored by Christian Parker, which I think will do wonders for him. Brian: It’s going to be difficult for certain players to shine in training camp due to the lack of physicality (tackling/hitting) in practices, so I’m going to have to go with a skill player here. I think second-year WR Traeshon Holdon could pick up where he left off last year in training camp where he turned some heads. He has another year in Brian Schottenheimer system and has been working with Dak Prescott. I think we’ll be hearing quite a bit from No. 80. Sean: I’m going to go with Shemar James, just because there is so much uncertainty around what he can bring to the defense, but a lot of potential as well. There’s been a laundry list of things to call a wash from last year’s defense and hope for better under Parker, and the overall communication on the backend of the defense under Eberflus was high on that list. James got “lost in the sauce” in this overall bad defense probably one too many times to have a lot of fans excited about him in Oxnard, but don’t forget how much legitimate smoke there was about the Cowboys drafting a traditional linebacker in the first round. That is still a roster need that’s been a little under-addressed, but if James starts turning the corner, it would go a long way. Is there any particular battle in training camp you’re keeping a close eye on, or one that Cowboys fans should be watching for this year? Mike: Shavon Revel against George Pickens. Pickens is a physical receiver who can challenge a corner at every level, making him the perfect daily test for measuring how far Revel has developed. Revel is also another year removed from his ACL injury, so he should look more confidence. There will inevitably be difficult reps against a receiver of Pickens’ quality, but that is exactly how Revel can accelerate his development. If he holds his own consistently, it would be an encouraging sign that he is ready to take a major step in the Cowboys’ secondary. Jess: The battle that has the most chance to decide wins or losses is at backup QB. Since 2020, Dak Prescott has missed five or more games every other season. He played a full 17 last year, so that’s daunting if the pattern holds. Sam Howell is now here to give Joe Milton real competition for the job. During some of Prescott’s absences, Cooper Rush reminded us how having a QB2 who can play competently can keep your season afloat. We need to see more of Howell and Milton to build our confidence that they can at least do that. Jorge: It’s the running back battle behind Javonte Williams for me. Each back, whether it’s Jaydon Blue, Phil Mafah, or Malik Davis, brings a different skill set to the table. The Dallas rushing attack was solid last year, and if one of the backs emerges behind Williams this offense could take another leap forward and make them even more lethal than last year’s unit. Brian: I’m going to cheat and go with two position battles we should all be watching closely, linebacker and left tackle. From a starting standpoint and a backup one, both positions remain unsettled right now heading into training camp. Both positions also carry some significant injury concerns for projected starters like Tyler Guyton and DeMarvion Overshown. Staying healthy and showing consistency at both positions will be key for the Cowboys success this year. Sean: I really like Jorge’s answer about the running backs, but I’m going to go with cornerback myself. We know Christian Parker will be working very closely and hands-on with this position group, so through the cornerback battle we’ll also learn about the new defensive coordinator. This is also a position group where the Cowboys had almost no choice but to keep some retreads from…

title: Cowboys news: Both coordinators are in the spotlight this year for Dallas
summary: Cowboys Could Soon Have Two of the NFL’s Hottest Head Coaching Candidates – Randy Gurzi, Cowboys on SI The Cowboys coordinators have a chance to establish themselves. Recently, Bryan Broaddus said he wasn’t sure Brian Schottenheimer was a “difference-maker” at head coach for the Dallas Cowboys. The well-respected insider did say, however, that Schottenheimer did well in […]
full_text: Cowboys Could Soon Have Two of the NFL’s Hottest Head Coaching Candidates – Randy Gurzi, Cowboys on SI The Cowboys coordinators have a chance to establish themselves. Recently, Bryan Broaddus said he wasn’t sure Brian Schottenheimer was a “difference-maker” at head coach for the Dallas Cowboys. The well-respected insider did say, however, that Schottenheimer did well in convincing the front office to change their approach and hire a younger defensive coordinator in Christian Parker . The selection of Parker highlights what makes Schottenheimer a strong leader. He knows how to evaluate and recruit talent, which is evident in the impressive staff he’s collected. That includes not only Parker and his assistant, but also a strong offensive staff led by offensive coordinator Klayton Adams. It’s easy to overlook Adams since Schottenheimer calls the plays, but he’s the driving force behind their impressive ground game. He’s also seen as a strong head coaching candidate in the future, as is Parker. Both are so highly regarded that The Athletic’s Jordan Rodrigue couldn’t decide which assistant had the better chance to become a star, so she named both Adams and Parker as breakout candidates in 2026. ”It was impossible to decide between second-year OC Adams and first-year DC Parker, who combine to make as exciting a coordinator tandem as we’ll see in 2026,” Rodrigue wrote. “Adams, a former offensive line coach, schematically blends modern, physical run concepts with a high-potential passing game. Parker is a disciple of storied Eagles defensive coordinator Vic Fangio, tasked with turning the Cowboys defense into a true threat — and those who have worked with Parker believe he can do it.” Cowboys Depth Chart: Is defensive tackle the best position group on the team? – Nick Harris, Fort Worth Star-Telegram When was the last time the Cowboys defensive tackle group was the best position group on defense? SAFE (5) Quinnen Williams, Kenny Clark, Otito Ogbonnia, Jonathan Bullard, LT Overton Is there a better defensive tackle group in the NFL than the Dallas Cowboys? A strong case could be made that the answer is no. After failing to land Quinnen Williams when they were shopping Micah Parsons last August, the Cowboys finally landed their big fish before the trade deadline for a first- and second-round pick. Now, the four-time Pro Bowler will look to return to his dominant ways for a defensive interior with a lot of potential. In seven games with the Cowboys last season, Williams accounted for 1.5 sacks and 21 total tackles. But now that he is able to participate fully in the offseason with his new teammates, the expectations are much higher for one of the team’s most prized possessions. A lot of the same things could be said for Kenny Clark, as he was uprooted from Green Bay less than a week before the start of the 2025 season when he was shipped to Dallas in the Parsons trade. While he did have some splash plays last season, the potential for Clark in 2026 is much higher with an actual runway to lead into the season with the offseason program and training camp. The large reshuffling in the defensive tackle room over the last year also includes trading away Osa Odighizuwa and Solomon Thomas in the span of an hour in April. Part of the thinking behind those moves was the confidence in new additions Otito Ogbonnia and Jonathan Bullard. Ogbonnia won’t be the pass rush world-beater that’s expected from others in the room (just a half-sack in four years in the NFL), but his run game value as a 3-tech makes him a useful rotational piece on early downs to allow the pass-rushing interior bodies to be fresher on passing downs. Bullard has positional flex in the interior with the ability to play anywhere from a true nose-tackle spot to the 5-tech spot just inside the tackle. An under-the-radar offseason addition for the Cowboys, Bullard’s 10 years of experience will give the rotational group a high floor in the interior. The positional versatility of rookie fourth-round pick LT Overton could fit him into multiple boxes, but we will place him into the defensive tackle mix for the sake of consistency. Expect Overton to be moved all around the defensive line, but the majority of his snaps should come as a hand-in-the-dirt defensive end with a pass-rushing outside linebacker on his outside shoulder. How does Caleb Downs live up to expectations? – Staff Writers, DallasCowboys.com There will be a lot riding on the shoulders of Caleb Downs as a rookie to help the defense. Tommy: By having a noticeable impact on the defense when he’s on the field. I know, you really can’t get more broad than that, but I’m not going to say he needs to be a Pro Bowler or an All-Pro in his rookie season. He doesn’t have to be. Would it be nice? Sure, but there are enough veterans on this defense to be able to help out around him as he gets his rookie season underway. Usually with defensive backs, the less you hear their name being called, the better the game they’re having. You certainly want that to be the case with Downs, but you also want to hear his name over the plays that everyone saw he can make while on the field at Ohio State. That’s what I mean by having a noticeable impact on the defense, and you’re welcome to define that however you want in your own personal expectations for Downs. Downs’ ceiling in this defense with Christian Parker is sky high. It seems like the two are almost replicas of one another when it comes to how they view and approach the game of football. I feel that’ll play a big part on Downs’ success early in his career. Will it be evident in Week 1? Maybe, maybe not, but Downs lives up to his first year expectations by being a plus player for this defense, because it’s a unit in need of a lot of plus players. Patrik : Living up to the status of being a first-round pick will always be a challenge, and especially if a team traded up in the top-15 to make sure they acquired you. Such is the case for Downs, but I don’t believe he’ll have much of an issue living up to his draft status, even if it takes a couple years. I won’t apply undue pressure in claiming he’ll somehow instantly be an All-Pro defensive back in Year 1, but I believe you’ll see plenty of flashes of that in his game. Downs feels different, in every way, in the last several weeks I’ve had to study his work ethic and demeanor. He’s already, almost instantly, become a locker room leader and that’s a large part of what he’ll be accountable for, so go ahead and check that box. What happens on the field will tell the full tale of what he can be in a Cowboys’ uniform, though. Do I expect Downs to be one of the MVPs of training camp, as a rookie? Yes, I actually do. I can easily see him making a list of plays that drop a few jaws, and his passion in-between the lines will be on full display as well. So, how does he live up to the mountain of expectations? By not staring at the mountain, and instead keep his eyes on the playbook and the next play — the rest will handle itself. The 3 biggest questions the Cowboys will need to answer in training camp – Connor Livesay, Blogging the Boys Tyler Guyton needs to have an outstanding training camp. Do the Cowboys have a starting left tackle on their roster? Another one of the biggest questions coming into training camp is who will win the starting left tackle job (the answer is Tyler Guyton)? While the safest bet here is Tyler Guyton will be the Cowboys starting left tackle when the Cowboys kick things off against the Giants, the bigger question is will he maintain control of the job for the entire season? Guyton did show some signs of development last season, before missing time due to injury, but injuries are something Guyton has dealt with in his first two years in the NFL. If Guyton is able to stay healthy, he will be serviceable at left tackle for the entire season, but the major question here is can he play most of the season? Nathan Thomas and rookie fifth-round pick Drew…

title: Lions mailbag, training camp edition: Who are the bubble players on OL, DL?
summary: Generally speaking, we have a pretty good idea of what the Detroit Lions’ starting offensive and defensive lines are going to look like for the 2026 season. While there will likely be a few training camp battles to weed out (left guard, EDGE2, and maybe right tackle), the key players have already been identified. However, […]
full_text: ARLINGTON, TX - OCTOBER 13: Mekhi Wingo #94 of the Detroit Lions walks off of the field after an NFL football game against the Dallas Cowboys at AT&T Stadium on October 13, 2024 in Arlington, Texas. (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images Generally speaking, we have a pretty good idea of what the Detroit Lions’ starting offensive and defensive lines are going to look like for the 2026 season. While there will likely be a few training camp battles to weed out (left guard, EDGE2, and maybe right tackle), the key players have already been identified. However, the depth at each position is very much up for grabs. This offseason, the Lions devoted a lot of resources to their offensive line reserves. They added Juice Scruggs, Ben Bartch, Larry Borom, and Seth McLaughlin to compete with the likes of Miles Frazier, Giovanni Manu, Michael Niese, and Colby Sorsdal, among others. Things are even more convoluted on the defensive side. With so many different roles on the line—nose tackle, 3-tech, “big” end, “rush” end, etc.—Detroit has several different archetypes who can fill one or multiple roles. Players like Ahmed Hassanein are switching positions from rush to big end, but is the competition there too competitive for the 2025 draft pick to make the roster? What does the drafting of Skyler Gill-Howard mean for the future of Mekhi Wingo? Is Levi Onwuzurike on the roster bubble given his injury history, or is he Detroit’s best option as a versatile backup to pretty much every position? Who will win the backup nose tackle job? And can Payton Turner turn his career around? On this week’s episode of the Midweek Mailbag, Erik Schlitt and I break down a lot of the roster bubble, which players are in competition for the same roster spot, and identify the different roles that Detroit needs to fill on both sides of the ball. Other topics on this week’s episode include (in chronological order): Will Kerby Joseph start training camp on the PUP list? Could Luke Altmyer realistically win the QB2 job or is he simply trying to make a case to keep a QB3? The things we’re most excited to see in training camp How will the preseason games change with no joint practices? Will Detroit be better prepared to start the season? Breaking down the pros/cons for the starting left guard candidates Which Lions player has the best odds to lead the entire NFL in a statistical category (ie: Jared Goff passing yards) Ranking the Lions’ seasons of the Dan Campbell era You can listen to the entire podcast using your favorite podcasting platform by searching “Pride of Detroit,” or you can use the embedded player below: Additionally, there’s a ton of bonus content from this episode if you want to watch the video version, which is available on our YouTube and Twitch pages .
